# OpenHikes repository instructions

## Build and test

The main project requires Xcode 26.5+, the iOS 26.0 platform, and a development team capable of signing the WeatherKit entitlement, the shared App Group, the iCloud container and the push entitlement. The shared package can be built and tested independently on macOS.

```sh
# Build the app and its embedded widget target
xcodebuild build \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run the two app-hosted unit bundles: the default local gate, ~20 seconds
xcodebuild test \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests

# Run everything the scheme's plan carries, UI automation included: ~13 minutes.
# This is not "the unit tests with extra safety" — OpenHikes.xctestplan lists
# OpenHikesUITests too, and omitting -only-testing: is the whole difference
# between a twenty-second gate and a quarter-hour one.
xcodebuild test \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run one app test suite or one test method
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss\(\)

# Run just the widget bundle
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests

# Run simulator UI automation and launch performance metrics
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikesUI \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 17 Pro'

# Run the standalone shared-package suite
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared

# Run one shared-package suite or test
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared --filter MercatorTests
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared \
  --filter 'OpenHikesSharedTests.MercatorTests/tileIndicesUnchanged'

# The shell scripts, against stubbed xcrun/xcodebuild/swiftlint/periphery
Scripts/run-script-tests.sh

# The Python: the report generator and the two CI gate programs
ruff check Scripts
python3 -m unittest discover --start-directory Scripts/tests
```

Scope the local test command the way CI does. The `unit-tests` job passes `-only-testing:OpenHikesTests -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests`, so an unscoped `xcodebuild test -scheme OpenHikes` is not the gate CI runs — it is that gate plus the whole `OpenHikesUITests` bundle, which turns roughly twenty seconds into roughly thirteen minutes of real gestures. Run the UI automation deliberately, through `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh`, where a bare `--all` parallelises by default: about thirteen minutes of serial test execution becomes 5m49s end to end, measured on a 16-core M-series machine.

Rebase before trusting a timing. A branch cut before a fix that made a suite faster keeps paying the old cost, and a measurement taken on it describes the branch rather than the change: long after `TrailBasemapRendererTests` had its snapshot boundary injected on `main`, a stale worktree here was still spending 570 seconds in `Trail basemap rendering` and reporting it as the cost of a full test run. The same applies to a suite that got *slower*: compare against `main` at the same commit, not against a number remembered from another branch.

Unit and integration tests use Swift Testing (`@Suite`, `@Test`, `#expect`). `-only-testing:` fails **silently** in two ways, both of which report a green run having executed nothing: an identifier it cannot resolve is ignored outright — which is what a suite declared inside an `extension` looks like, so `-only-testing:OpenHikesTests/BackgroundDeliveryTests` selects nothing because that suite lives in `extension WidgetFeedSuites` — and a Swift Testing *method* needs its trailing `()`, so `…/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss` runs zero tests while `…/elevationGainAndLoss()` runs it. Neither produces a warning. Any job that pins a list of `-only-testing:` entries must therefore read the result bundle and assert what actually ran rather than trust `xcodebuild`'s exit status, as the `thread-sanitizer` job does: an exact suite count, because the pinned list is fixed and a fall means an identifier stopped resolving, and a floor rather than an exact count for tests, which rise whenever anyone writes one. The `OpenHikesUITests` simulator bundle uses XCTest/XCUITest because Apple's UI automation and performance metrics are not available through Swift Testing. The main `xcodebuild test` action runs the two app-hosted bundles, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`, plus `OpenHikesUITests`; the dedicated `OpenHikesUI` scheme runs only UI automation. `OpenWidgetTests` compiles the `OpenWidget/` sources into itself, since an app extension cannot host a test bundle.

App tests use the in-memory SwiftData fixtures in `OpenHikesTests/General/TestSupport.swift`. A suite that touches the tile pipeline builds a `TileSandbox` — its own `TileCache` directories and its own `AutoSaveTileStore` — rather than `TileCache.shared`; the singletons belong to the app, and the whole bundle shares one process. Likewise `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `LocationManager` and `OfflineTileDownloader` take injectable location, defaults, clock and transport, so no test depends on wall-clock time, a real connection, or the host app's settings.

UI-test app launches pass `--ui-testing`, which selects an in-memory SwiftData store and isolated `UserDefaults`. Additional launch arguments can expand the sheet (`--ui-test-expanded-sheet`), enable real simulator Core Location (`--ui-test-enable-location`), import a bundled GPX fixture (`--ui-test-import-gpx=ThumseeLoopFast`), match against a bundled trail graph instead of Overpass (`--ui-test-trail-graph=ThumseeRidgePath`), give the tile cache its own empty storage root and no network monitor so every tile is a genuine miss (`--ui-test-offline`), seed a hike with generated photos (`--ui-test-seed-photos=<count>`), with a finished walk (`--ui-test-seed-walks=HalfLoop`, the one fixture `SeededWalkFixture` knows) or the field-metrics store with reports (`--ui-test-seed-metrics=<count>`), fail the first save of a finished recording so the retry path is reachable (`--ui-test-fail-first-save`), stand an import on the losing side of the selection race it would otherwise win (`--ui-test-lose-import-selection`), serve a fixed forecast instead of WeatherKit (`--ui-test-weather`), grant the paid-map entitlement without StoreKit (`--ui-test-entitled`), seed a fake photo library (`--ui-test-photo-library=<count>`), or open a performance log for a named scenario (`--ui-test-performance-log=<scenario>`). Every one of them is `DEBUG`-only and takes effect only alongside `--ui-testing`; `AppLaunchEnvironment` is the single source of truth for all of them, and a new one belongs there and in this list beside the rest. XCUITest drives static locations through `XCUIDevice.shared.location`; longer route playback remains available through `Scripts/simulate-hike.sh`. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` boots one UI test (`--test`), one class (`--suite … --all`) or every functional class (`--all`) against a named simulator; `--list` prints them as `Class/method`. A bare `--all` hands the fan-out to `xcodebuild`, which clones the resolved device and spreads the *classes* across the clones. That is the default rather than a flag because `--all` is the line the PR template, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` all already tell a contributor to run, and an opt-in nobody types is an opt-in nobody gets. Three workers, because the floor of a parallel run is its longest class: `RecordingUITests` is 274s of a 787s serial `--all`, three already reach that floor, and a fourth only adds a device to contend with. `--serial` returns to one simulator and `--parallel N` overrides the count; the two contradict each other and passing both is an error. Anything narrower than a bare `--all` stays serial with no comment, since a run scoped to one class or one method has nothing to spread — that is also what keeps the `accessibility-ui-tests` job on a single device, because it always passes `--suite`, and an explicit `--parallel` there is refused rather than quietly downgraded. The performance suite has no such flag and must not gain one — it reads its logs back through `simctl get_app_container` on the one resolved UDID, which a clone is not, and a measurement taken on a contended machine describes the machine. Fixtures, launch helpers and gestures shared by the bundle live in `OpenHikesUITests/UITestSupport.swift`, and the audit types, MapKit filter and report formatting in `OpenHikesUITests/AccessibilityAuditSupport.swift` — reuse them rather than re-deriving a coordinate or a wait. The bundle is split by subject, one class per file because SwiftLint's `single_test_class` requires it: `OpenHikesUITests` (map, sheet, hike details), `OrientationUITests`, `RecordingUITests`, `WalkUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests`, `AccessibilityLabelUITests` and `PerformanceUITests`.

`PerformanceUITests` is a measurement suite rather than a correctness one. `--ui-test-performance-log=<scenario>` makes `PerformanceLog` write every signpost mark and interval, every `MainThreadWatchdog` stall and a 1 Hz CPU/footprint/power sample to `Documents/PerformanceLogs/<scenario>.tsv`; the test additionally sets `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` in `launchEnvironment`, since a test plan's environment reaches the runner and not the app. Because the test is out of process, it reads live counters through the `performance-counters` accessibility probe. `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` runs the suite, pulls the TSVs with `simctl get_app_container`, and renders a report through `Scripts/perf-report.py`. Baseline numbers and the open work live in `PERFORMANCE.md`.

Two `xcodebuild test` runs cannot share a simulator. They install the same bundle identifier onto the same device, so the second install tears the first run's app out from under it, and the failure arrives as `Test crashed with signal kill` landing on whichever test happened to be executing — a different one each time, with no assertion and no diagnostic. Under load it also arrives as `kAXErrorServerNotFound`, `Application … is not running`, or a run that dies before any test starts. Four separate investigations this repository has run mistook that signature for a product bug, and one of them measured load average 101–180 while chasing it. If a run fails *differently* each time, or fails in an area nobody touched, suspect the device before the code: create a private device with `xcrun simctl create`, target it by UDID, and delete it afterwards — `--device` on both scripts takes a UDID as well as a name, and either way resolves to exactly one device that the destination and every `simctl` call then share. A green run on a contended simulator is no more trustworthy than a red one. The parallel `--all` is not an exception to any of this but an application of it: the fan-out belongs to `xcodebuild`, which gives each worker its own cloned device rather than letting two runs collide on one, and it clones *from* the device resolved above, so the cleared location and any `simctl privacy` grant made beforehand are inherited by every worker.

Neither the functional UI automation nor the performance suite runs in CI both drive a booted simulator through real gestures and timing-sensitive waits, which a shared runner makes slow and flaky, and the performance suite needs stable hardware for its numbers to mean anything. The accessibility classes are the exception: the `accessibility-ui-tests` job runs `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` through `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh --suite <class> --all --retry` — the `--suite` is load-bearing beyond selection, since it is what keeps a shared runner on one simulator rather than cloning three, granting location with `simctl privacy` up front so the two location-dependent tests never see a permission alert. That job ran `continue-on-error: true` from 2026-08-15 to 2026-09-06 while its flake rate was measured, and the trial is over: 192 completed runs, zero failures at the job level and at the step level both, so it now fails the workflow like every other job. The number and its one caveat — it is a *post-retry* rate, and `--retry` makes a test that passed on its second attempt indistinguishable from one that passed on its first — are recorded beside the job in `ci.yml` rather than only here. `PerformanceUITests` is listed in `skippedTests` for `OpenHikes.xctestplan`, so `xcodebuild test -scheme OpenHikes` does not pay for it; the `OpenHikesUI` scheme autocreates its plan and therefore still sees it, which is how `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` selects it. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` names its functional classes explicitly — today `OpenHikesUITests`, `RecordingUITests`, `WalkUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` — for the same reason, so a new class has to be added to that list to be reachable through the script, and its `measurement_tests` list keeps `testLaunchPerformance` out of `--all` while still allowing `--test testLaunchPerformance`. A new UI test class added to that bundle inherits none of this and must be placed on the correct side of it.

Three things that suite learned the hard way. Absolute memory readings taken under XCUITest are automation overhead, not the app's footprint — the same build launched by `simctl` sits substantially lower, so only compare footprints within a run. The first hit-test against a newly presented screen makes SwiftUI evaluate bodies, so a phase must warm the accessibility tree before it starts counting or it is charged for the previous screen. And `stopMeasuring()` truncates `XCTApplicationLaunchMetric`'s signpost interval, which makes `harvestData` raise rather than report; let the measure block end on its own.

A UI test that spoofs a route has to respect `RecordingFixPolicy`: a static simulated location is delivered once, so a fix rejected for implied speed or displacement has to be set again, and the test waits on the `recording-point-count` element rather than on a fixed sleep. Accessibility identifiers belong on the leaf views automation taps — SwiftUI pushes a container's identifier down onto every descendant, which would leave a whole screen answering to one name.

A suite that genuinely cannot run without an environment capability (today: the App Group container) stays conditionally enabled, but must report the skip through `SuitePrecondition`; strict mode turns a missing precondition into a failure — `xcodebuild test … "SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS=\$(inherited) REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES"` from a command line, or `OPENHIKES_REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES=1` in the scheme's test action from Xcode (a simulator-hosted test bundle inherits nothing from the invoking shell, which is why there are two).

Seven jobs can fail the workflow — `Lint and shared package`, `App and widget tests`, `iOS Debug build`, `iOS Release build`, `Unsigned iOS archive`, `Thread sanitizer` and `Accessibility UI tests` — and all of them hang off a `changes` job that decides whether a pull request touched anything but `**/*.md`, `LICENSE` and `docs/`. A documentation-only pull request skips them and merges. Failing the workflow is not yet the same as blocking a merge, and this file used to claim otherwise: `main`'s branch protection lists no `required_status_checks` at all, so a red run is an annotation nobody is required to read — #182 and #185 both merged with `Thread sanitizer` red. Naming the seven there is a repository-settings change rather than a workflow one, and until it is made, "gates a merge" anywhere in this file means "reports red". The filtering is deliberately a job-level `if:` rather than a `paths-ignore:` on the trigger: a required check belonging to a workflow that never ran stays at "Expected" forever and blocks the merge outright, while a skipped *job* reports success. The list is an allow-list, so an unrecognised path counts as code and one code file among any number of prose ones runs everything; adding a new non-compiling path there is a deliberate act, not a tidy-up. A push to `main` and a manual dispatch always build everything.

Lint with `Scripts/lint.sh` (`--fix` applies what SwiftLint can correct). It runs strict SwiftLint at the version pinned in `.swiftlint-version`, and the CI `quality` job invokes that same script, so local and CI results cannot drift. It exits 0 clean, **2** for violations found and **1** for "could not run" — the third case exists because a `.swiftlint.yml` that fails to parse is only a *warning* to SwiftLint, which then lints on against the default configuration and can report a clean run having read no config at all.

The Xcode build also lints, through SwiftLintPlugins' `SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin` attached to `OpenHikes`, `OpenWidgetExtension`, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`. It runs `swiftlint lint --quiet --force-exclude` — no `--strict`, and at the version the package resolves to rather than the one in `.swiftlint-version` — so every *warning*-severity violation is invisible to it, and `Scripts/lint.sh` is what a change has to pass. An *error*-severity violation is the opposite: the plugin is a **prebuild** command, SwiftLint exits 2, and the target fails before a single file is compiled, which takes `build-for-testing` down for all four targets at once. So the error-severity rules are not advisory, they are a build gate, and these are the thresholds a large file or a branchy function actually trips: `file_length` 900, `cyclomatic_complexity` 18, `type_body_length` 450, `function_body_length` 90, `closure_body_length` 80, `line_length` 160, `identifier_name` 2–70 characters, `function_parameter_count` 9, `large_tuple` 4, and — inherited from SwiftLint's defaults rather than named in `.swiftlint.yml` — `enum_case_associated_values_count` 6. Nine more are error on a *single* occurrence: `attribute_name_spacing`, `duplicate_conditions`, `duplicate_enum_cases`, `dynamic_inline`, `force_cast`, `force_try`, `invisible_character`, `shorthand_operator` and `unhandled_throwing_task`. None of this is visible in `.swiftlint.yml`, which contains no literal `severity: error` line.

What keeps a scratch copy of the tree out of the lint is `included:`, not `excluded:` — SwiftLint's directory walk does **not** skip dot-directories, so a git worktree or a plain copy at the repository root is lintable material. `included:` stops applying the moment an explicit path is passed on the command line, which is exactly how the plugin invokes it, so `excluded:` carries `"**/.*"` as the durable guard rather than the name of whichever scratch directory exists today. `Scripts/install-git-hooks.sh` installs an opt-in pre-push hook. There is no formatting command.

Three optional tools are used if installed and skipped if not; the README lists the `brew install` line. `xcbeautify` formats `xcodebuild` output, and `Scripts/lib/xcodebuild-output.sh` is the one place that decides how — both UI scripts source it, and it falls back to their previous `grep` filter on a machine without it. Its constraint is load-bearing and is why those scripts still keep a raw log: xcbeautify prints nothing at all for output it cannot parse, which covers `measured [...]` lines, indented `PERF-` markers, ThreadSanitizer race reports, and any test failure with no recognised diagnostic — a crash or a hang produces no formatted line, not even `** TEST FAILED **`. It understands Swift Testing, so a failing `@Test` keeps its issue text and `file:line`. CI pipes every `xcodebuild` and `swift test` call through it under `--renderer github-actions` except the TSan job, whose raw report is the product; each of those `run:` blocks needs `set -o pipefail`, because Actions runs `bash -e` without it and would otherwise report the formatter's exit status rather than xcodebuild's. `Scripts/periphery.sh` runs `periphery scan` against `.periphery.yml` at the version pinned in `.periphery-version` and reports unreferenced declarations; it is not in CI because it rebuilds the project with indexing enabled, and its report is candidates to read rather than a verdict — `--exclude-tests` finds the declarations only tests use, at the cost of listing every deliberate test seam alongside them. That pin is checked as an error rather than the warning `Scripts/lint.sh` settles for, because Periphery 2.x reads none of this configuration and says so about only part of it: `--targets` was still required for an `.xcodeproj`, `retain_equatable_properties` and `retain_hashable_properties` did not exist before 3.8.0 and are reported as `invalid key`, and — because every target in `OpenHikes.xcodeproj` is an Xcode synchronized folder group rather than a list of file references — a 2.x scan with `--targets` supplied by hand indexes no Swift file at all and prints "No unused code detected" having read none of the code. The script fails a run whose output carries any of those, for the same reason `Scripts/lint.sh` fails a lint that fell back to SwiftLint's defaults. `xcode-build-server config -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes` regenerates `buildServer.json`, which is what lets `sourcekit-lsp` resolve symbols in the app target rather than only in the shared package; it holds absolute paths, so it is gitignored and is regenerated after adding or renaming a target.

That plugin only runs once its package fingerprint is trusted, and the trust lives per user in `~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm/security/plugins.json`, outside the repository — so a fresh CI machine fails with `Plugin "SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin" ... must be enabled before it can be used`. The checked-in `AllowedPackagePlugins.json` covers opening the project locally; CI does not read it. Every `xcodebuild` call in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` therefore passes `-skipPackagePluginValidation`, and a new one must too. Xcode Cloud composes its own `xcodebuild` invocation and cannot take that flag, so `ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` — which Xcode Cloud runs by name after cloning — sets `IDESkipPackagePluginFingerprintValidatation` (Apple's typo, not ours) and `IDESkipMacroFingerprintValidation` instead. Adding a package that ships a build tool plugin or a macro needs no further change; removing the SwiftLint plugin would make all of it dead weight.

`AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are the VoiceOver suites. The first sweeps `performAccessibilityAudit` per screen and the second asserts the labels, values and traits the app promises, because the audit cannot know that a provider row is the selected one or that the elevation graph should speak the point under the tracker. It runs with `.contrast`, `.textClipped` and `.dynamicType` subtracted — each exclusion is argued next to it, and `.dynamicType` in particular reports SwiftUI nodes it cannot introspect, including a navigation bar's own "Done" button. Issues whose detail names an `MK`-prefixed class are MapKit's and are filtered rather than fixed. Widening either exclusion needs the same argument; an audit that starts failing on a view the app does draw is a real regression.

A test that provokes a `nonisolated` delegate callback must wait through `settleDelegateHop(until:)` in `OpenHikesTests/General/SettleSupport.swift`, naming the effect it expects, rather than spinning a fixed number of `Task.yield()`s. A yield count buys an amount of progress that depends on machine load — which is how `Map coordinator` and `Location publishing` went red on CI while passing locally. Both unit bundles are `parallelizable: false` in `OpenHikes.xctestplan`, which is what makes those deadlines mean anything: the bundle is main-actor isolated project-wide, so Swift Testing's in-process parallelism could never run two tests at once, only interleave a thousand of them at their suspension points against one executor. Run 33049137656 is what that cost — seven recording tests starved together, and a five-second budget took seventeen seconds of wall time to notice it had expired. Serializing is the fix; a bigger budget is not. The condition-less overload is best-effort only, and a bare settle is almost always dead code now: because the delegate bodies deliver through `onMainActor`, a stub's `deliver(...)` runs the callback synchronously before it returns, so an assertion reading a synchronous effect (`stats`, `phase`, `trace`, a stub counter) needs no settle at all. Keep a *conditioned* settle wherever the effect is genuinely deferred — a journal flush, live matching, a shared widget snapshot, trail-graph prefetch state, the review preview, or `locationManagerDidChangeAuthorization`, which still hops explicitly because it awaits. The same rule bans a fixed `Task.sleep` as a barrier: wait on the positive effect that must follow, then assert the thing you are denying never happened.

## Architecture

- Following Apple's Food Truck and Backyard Birds samples, `OpenHikes/` is organized by product domain rather than generic `Managers`, `Models`, and `Views` layers. `App/` is the composition root; `Hikes/`, `Recording/`, `Map/`, `Tiles/`, `Photos/`, `Weather/`, `Purchases/`, `Sync/`, and `Settings/` own their related models, services, and views.
- `OpenHikesApp` creates one `OpenHikesModel` and injects it through the SwiftUI environment. That model owns the single `ModelContainer` plus long-lived location, weather, background tracking, auto-save, cloud sync, and recording dependencies; `OpenHikesView` owns transient selection, map presentation, and navigation state. `Hike` is the persisted source of truth, while `RouteProfile` is the precomputed distance/elevation index used by both chart scrubbing and GPS route matching. Stopping a recording that the matcher moved or found ambiguous ends in `.reviewing` rather than in the store: `RouteReviewSection.sections(in:)` groups the per-fix legs into reviewable sections, `RecordingRouteReview` holds the per-section `TrailRouteChoice`, and only `saveReviewedRecording()` writes the `Hike`.
- The map is an imperative MapKit subsystem behind `MapView`. `MapView.Coordinator` observes stable controller objects and updates `MKMapView` directly. Tile drawing flows through `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `TileOverlay` into `TileCache`; passive durable saves go through `AutoSaveTileStore`, while policy-permitted bulk downloads go through `OfflineTileDownloader`.
- `Community/` is the one part of the app that writes to a database other people read, and is deliberately separate from `Sync/`. `Sync/` reports on SwiftData's mirroring of the hiker's own hikes into their **private** CloudKit database; `Community/` is hand-written `CKRecord` work against the **public** database of the same container, with its own transport protocol, its own record types, and no contact with the `ModelContainer` at all. `CommunityPublisher` uploads a hike, `CommunityBrowser` holds what the searched area found, `CommunityQueryPolicy` decides whether a pan is worth *offering* to re-ask about, `CommunitySearchArea` is the circle one answer covers, `CommunityAreaName` says what to call it, `MapCommunityAnnotations` draws the results on the map that asked and `MapCommunitySearchControl` is the *Search this area* button, `MapCommunityRoutes` draws where each of those results actually *goes* — `CommunityRouteOutline` is the kilobyte-sized copy of a route that makes that affordable to fetch and `CommunityRouteHitTest` is what turns a tap on one of those lines into a hike, since MapKit hit-tests annotations and never overlays, `CommunityPageBudget` decides how many pages one request may spend once blocked rows are taken out of it, `CommunityImport` turns a published hike into an ordinary `Hike`, `CommunityReport` composes the message a hiker reports one with — which reaches the reviewer by mail rather than through the transport, for the reason given below — and `CommunityBlockList` holds the authors this device has hidden, which is the browse lists' filter and needs no account, no network and no record type of its own. See *The community feature* below for the two record types and why there are two.
- `OpenHikesShared` is a local Swift package consumed by the app and iOS widget. Its source and tests mirror the `Recording/`, `Trails/`, `Widget/`, `LiveActivity/`, and `General/` domains; put cross-target payloads, projections, deep links, and shared presentation logic there rather than duplicating them in targets.
- The app precomputes a compact `SharedTrailSnapshot`, writes it atomically through `SharedStore`, and reloads widget timelines. The iOS widget reads that App Group store directly and never recomputes route matching — but it does read location, deliberately, which the next bullet describes. Both snapshots use the current wire format described in *Schema and migration policy*. Every version mismatch or decode failure is reported as a `SharedStoreDiagnostic` to the `OpenHikes`/`SharedStore` log with the offending key and coding path named; the shared package uses `os.Logger` because `RenderSignpost` is app-target-only. `TrailBasemapSet` carries no version deliberately — it is regenerable derived state, so a schema change costs one render rather than a blank widget — but its decode failures are reported the same way, because an undecodable manifest re-renders forever. A partly failed render pass publishes the images that did land rather than discarding all four: the four snapshots are four separate requests, and the widget picks one image by shape and appearance, so a set holding the one it is being asked for draws a map where an all-or-nothing set draws the line glyph. That is only safe because `refreshIfNeeded`'s short-circuit asks `TrailBasemapRenderer.holdsEveryCombination(_:)` as well — its other three questions (same coverage, images on disk, intended scale) are all asked of the manifest's *own* images, so without it a manifest holding three of four would be accepted as done forever and the missing combination would fall back to the line glyph until the trail's geometry changed.
- The widget *does* read location, and that is a shipped feature rather than an oversight: `OpenWidget/Info.plist` declares `NSWidgetWantsLocation` and `TrailWidget.swift` owns `WidgetRecordingLocationSampler`, which drops the sparse anchors the README advertises into a live recording so the app can repair a GPS gap it slept through. It is fenced in on every side. The timeline provider asks for a fix only when the stored `SharedRecordingSnapshot` says `isCapturingFixes`, and awaits it best-effort — a timeline is owed whether or not a fix arrives, so both paths end in `Self.currentTimeline()` and the entry is re-read from the store afterwards. The sampler itself refuses unless `CLLocationManager.isAuthorizedForWidgetUpdates` holds and the status is `.authorizedAlways` or `.authorizedWhenInUse`, takes at most one fix per 15 minutes through `SharedStore.claimRecordingWidgetSample` — a lock-file claim in the App Group rather than an in-process timer, because a widget process is short-lived and there can be several — and gives up after 8 seconds. `WidgetRecordingRequest.consume()` is what makes the race between an arriving fix and that timeout resume the continuation exactly once, which is the precondition `withCheckedContinuation` needs. A fix that survives `WidgetRecordingFixPolicy` — at most 5 minutes old, horizontal accuracy between 0 and 200 m, Mercator-representable — is appended through `PendingRecordingFixStore.append(_:validatingRecordingAt:)`, which re-reads the snapshot under the same lock and drops the fix if the session changed or the recording stopped meanwhile; the queue is `pending-fixes.json`, capped at 200 entries oldest-first. Elevation rides along only when `verticalAccuracy` is within 30 m, course and speed only when non-negative.
- That hand-off is one-way, and the widget's half of it is append-only: it never reads the queue back, never matches a route and never computes a statistic, which is the boundary it really keeps. `HikeRecorder.mergePendingWidgetFixes(for:)` drains it — `AppGroupRecordingSharedStateStore.pendingFixes(for:)` filters to the live session off-main, `journalQueue.drain()` settles the journal first so the merge sees every fix already accepted, `TrackJournal.mergeWidgetFixes` deduplicates against the journal's timestamps within 5 seconds, and `removePendingFixes(ids:)` clears what merged. Failing that last clear is logged rather than fatal on purpose: the journal merge is already durable, and the next drain deduplicates the copies left behind.
- The Live Activity is split across all three targets along the same seam the widget is. `OpenHikesShared/LiveActivity/` owns `HikeActivityAttributes` — the payload — plus its content builders and `HikeActivityPresentation`, which decides every word, rounding and chip on both surfaces and is the testable half of the UI. `OpenWidget/` draws it. `OpenHikes/LiveActivity/` decides *when* one exists. The payload is a plain `Codable, Hashable, Sendable` struct and its `ActivityAttributes` conformance lives alone in `HikeActivityAttributes+ActivityKit.swift` behind `#if os(iOS)`: ActivityKit *is* importable on macOS, but `ActivityAttributes`, `Activity` and `ActivityContent` are all `@available(macOS, unavailable)`, so `canImport` is the wrong guard and the package's macOS support — which is what lets `swift test` run the shared package's test suite on a Mac in CI — would otherwise have to go. The attributes *type name* is a storage contract: ActivityKit identifies a running activity by it, so renaming the type orphans every activity already on screen.
- A Live Activity never reads the App Group store, a location or a route profile; it renders `context.state` and nothing else, exactly as the widget renders its snapshot. Both surfaces are fed from the same two funnels the widget is fed from — `HikeRecorder.publishSharedRecordingSnapshot(force:)` and `BackgroundTrailTracker.updateStoredLiveFix` — so the two can only ever disagree about a *rate*, never about a fact. The polyline is deliberately left out of the payload: attributes plus `ContentState` share a 4 KB budget, and `payloadFitsTheActivityBudget` asserts it. `ContentState` carries `elapsedSeconds` and `updatedAt` so the view can derive a `timerStart` and hand the ticking to `Text(timerInterval:)`, which the system advances without spending an ActivityKit update; `RunState` is what says whether that timer may run, because a `Text(timerInterval:)` cannot be stopped once drawn.
- **A hike's name is bounded where it is entered, not where it is spent** (`Hikes/HikeTitle.swift`). It is the only free text the app carries from a person or a file into the 4 KB payload above, and `HikeTitle.bounded(_:)` is the one place the rule lives — the rename field, the Stop alert's name field (through `HikeRecorder.normalizedCustomName`) and the GPX importer (through `HikeTitle.imported(trackName:fileURL:)`) all go through it, and a new way to name a hike has to as well. Both bounds are load-bearing: 128 characters *and* 512 UTF-8 bytes, because a grapheme cluster has no length limit, so a character count alone would let one `Character` of ten thousand combining marks through — not a thing anybody types, which is exactly why an unattended `Documents/Inbox` file is what it is for. The shared package's `HikeActivityTests` measures its worst case at 498 bytes against these numbers and cannot import the app to check them, so the two move together.
- Target folders are Xcode file-system-synchronized groups. New Swift files under `OpenHikes/`, `OpenHikesTests/`, `OpenHikesUITests/`, `OpenWidget/`, or `OpenWidgetTests/` are discovered by their corresponding targets; place files in the target that should compile them. `OpenWidget/` is synchronized into two targets — the extension and `OpenWidgetTests` — with `OpenWidgetBundle.swift` excluded from the latter, since a test bundle must not carry a second `@main`. A folder synchronized into a target has its *resources* bundled too, and flat — which is why `OpenHikes/SimulatedLocations/` needs `EXCLUDED_SOURCE_FILE_NAMES = "*/SimulatedLocations/*"` on the app target's **Release** configuration alone. The four fixtures there are read from `Bundle.main` by `--ui-test-import-gpx=` and `--ui-test-trail-graph=`, so Debug must keep them and a shipped build must not carry test data it has no `#if DEBUG` code left to read. `OpenHikes.storekit` is the same question answered a different way: it is not in the synchronized folder at all, so it was in the app's Resources phase by hand and is now in neither — the scheme's `StoreKitConfigurationFileReference` names it by path and never wanted it copied into the product. What keeps both out is project configuration, which fails silently; CI's archive job asserts the absence, reading the fixture names off the folder so a fifth one is covered on the day it is added.

## Repository-specific conventions

- Preserve render isolation. High-frequency GPS, sheet, chart-scrub, route-styling, and map-command state lives in stable `@Observable` reference types such as `RouteHighlight`, `SheetMetrics`, `RouteStyle`, `MapController`, `TrackerState`, and `LocationManager`. Parent SwiftUI bodies must not read their changing properties; `MapView.Coordinator` uses `withObservationTracking` to update only MapKit. Use `RenderSignpost` and the `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` scheme variable when changing this flow.
- UI and SwiftData coordination are main-actor isolated. Delegate callbacks are `nonisolated` and reach that state through `onMainActor { ... }` in `General/MainActorDelivery.swift`, which runs the body synchronously via `MainActor.assumeIsolated` when the callback already arrived on the main thread and falls back to `Task { @MainActor in ... }` when it did not. Every `CLLocationManager` here is created on the main actor, so its deliveries take the synchronous path — which is what removes a heap allocation per GPS fix across three live delegates, and what restores ordering between consecutive batches, since two separate unstructured tasks on one actor have no defined order and a reordered pair is silently dropped by `RecordingFixPolicy`'s `interval > 0` guard. A callback that has to `await` (authorization changes, `withObservationTracking` re-arming) keeps the explicit `Task { @MainActor in ... }`; a `withObservationTracking` `onChange` **must** stay deferred, since it fires mid-mutation. Tile math, image encoding, disk enumeration, and other blocking pipeline work stay off the main thread; existing hot paths call `assertOffMainThread`. Keep shared off-main types `Sendable` and protect mutable singleton state with the existing lock pattern.
- Going the *other* way needs `Task.detached` or a `nonisolated` function, never a bare `Task {}`. A `Task {}` started from a method on a `@MainActor` type inherits that isolation and runs its body on the main thread, so any synchronous call inside it blocks the UI while looking exactly like offloaded work. This shipped once: `CloudSyncCoordinator` built its `CKContainer` inside such a task, and CloudKit's framework load and daemon handshake pinned the main thread for seconds on a fresh install — a grey map, no sheet, and an unresponsive app on a new user's first launch. `CloudSyncCoordinator.offMainThread(_:)` is the guarded seam and `CloudSyncCoordinatorTests` fails if either safeguard is removed. Making a property `lazy` does not help: it changes *when* the work runs, not *where*. A bare `nonisolated` *function* is only half the escape, and the other half is the one that bites: `SWIFT_APPROACHABLE_CONCURRENCY` makes a `nonisolated async` function `nonisolated(nonsending)`, so it runs on its caller's executor — a main-actor caller means a main-thread body. Say `@concurrent` on the callee, and on a protocol *requirement* when the off-main-ness is part of the contract rather than of one conformance. `PhotoLibraryWriting.save` is why that is written down: it cost a `MainThreadWatchdog` stall for PhotoKit's first-touch handshake and, worse, a crash — a `performChanges` block formed inside a main-actor body inherits main-actor isolation, PhotoKit runs it on `com.apple.PHPhotoLibrary.changes`, and the isolation check Swift emits at the top of it trapped every mirrored save. `PhotoLibraryMirrorTests.mirroringStaysOffTheMainActor` reads the executor the stub's body actually woke up on, and the stub stays free of `@concurrent` so it cannot pass by hopping under its own power.
- Respect tile-provider policy. `TileProvider.supportsBulkDownload` gates prefetching: OpenStreetMap is passive auto-save only. Tile identity is provider plus zoom/x/y and nothing else — display scale is deliberately absent, because no provider template substitutes one and both paths therefore fetch identical bytes; `TileCacheKey` defines the shared spelling for the renderer and downloader. When deleting durable tiles, use `TileOwnership` so tiles shared by multiple hikes are not removed.
- Present modals from inside the sheet's *contents*, not beside the presentation. `OpenHikesView` keeps `MapSheet` presented permanently in portrait and puts it back if it is ever dismissed, so a `.sheet`, `.fullScreenCover`, `.photosPicker` or `.fileImporter` attached to the same view as that sheet is never presented at all — no error, just a button that does nothing. `MapSheet`'s `.fileImporter`, and the `.photoCapturePickers` and `.weatherDetailSheet` on `OpenHikesView.mapSheet()`, are inside for this reason; alerts are the exception and stay on the root view, where they survive the sheet being rebuilt. "Inside the contents" rather than "inside the sheet" is what keeps one answer right in both shapes below: in landscape there is no sheet to be beside.
- **The primary surface has two shapes, and landscape is not the sheet.** `.presentationDetents` are honoured only in a compact-width, *regular*-height presentation, so in compact height — iPhone landscape — the system ignores them and presents the sheet full-screen. For a sheet that is never taken down that is not a taller sheet but the whole UI, with the map behind it and nothing that brings it back; it shipped that way, and `OrientationUITests` is what stops it coming back. `MapSidePanel` is drawn beside the map instead — an ordinary overlay, not a presentation, holding the same `MapSheet` — while `SheetPresentation.layout` resolves what the two shapes disagree about, so no screen inside the sheet asks which one it is in. **`verticalSizeClass` is read in `SheetLayoutReader` and nowhere else**, and that is a render-isolation rule rather than tidiness: an `@Environment` read in `OpenHikesView`'s body re-runs it whenever SwiftUI thinks the value may have moved, which a scene transition does — measured as one extra root body pass per transition (`testBackgroundRecordingCostsNothingPerFix` fails by exactly that one), the map update that follows it, and 250-odd tile requests in an offline browse budgeted for none. The flag it publishes changes on a rotation and at no other time. For the same reason the sheet is presented from `$showSheet` rather than from a `Binding` built in the body, which is a new binding on every pass and re-runs the sheet's content with it. Two things follow. The map's own controls hang off a layout guide the panel's width is spent on (`MapView.sidePanelInset` → `Coordinator.controlsLeadingConstraint`), because `additionalSafeAreaInsets` belongs to `UIViewController` and this map is a `UIView`. The camera's route fitting spends that same occupied width on the physical leading edge, including the panel's safe-area margin. **Only the map may ignore the horizontal safe area**: the weather overlay and panel share the window's safe leading edge, while the badge ignores only the vertical safe area so `WeatherBadge.topPadding` still agrees with `MapView.addAttribution`. `OpenHikesApp`'s scene root keeps the safe area. `SheetPresentation` retains each destination's `HikeDetailInteraction` and `PhotoViewerSelection` until its route is popped, so replacing the host on rotation preserves the selected section, rename draft and current photo; these objects are read by the destination, never by the root or sheet bodies.
- Files written outside SwiftData need an owner and a sweep. Photo and tile deletion is fire-and-forget, so termination can leave files with nothing pointing at them; `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` and `HikePhotoStore.reclaimOrphans(claimedBy:)` are the backstops, both driven at launch from a *complete* claim set — a fetch that fails must sweep nothing rather than sweep with an empty set.
- **A program inside YAML is a program nothing checks.** Anything a workflow decides with more than a shell conditional goes in a file under `Scripts/`, not in a `python3 - <<'PY'` heredoc: the coverage floor and the ThreadSanitizer suite-count gate spent months as heredocs, where no parser read them, nothing linted them and no test could reach them, while one of them could fail a merge. They are `Scripts/check-coverage-floor.py` and `Scripts/check-sanitized-selection.py` now, and the pins they enforce stay in the workflow as environment variables, next to the comments that argue for the numbers. Python is held to the same standard as the shell: the `quality` job parse-checks every `*.py` under `Scripts/` and `ci_scripts/` the way it parse-checks every `*.sh`, `ruff` is pinned in `.ruff-version` and configured in `ruff.toml` exactly as SwiftLint is pinned in `.swiftlint-version`, and the suite in `Scripts/tests/` runs against the real files rather than a copy — a script whose name is not an identifier is loaded by path through `Scripts/tests/loader.py`.
- `TileCache` intentionally has memory, ephemeral cache, and durable Application Support tiers. Do not turn a render miss into synchronous disk/network work, and do not move expensive storage measurement into a SwiftUI body.
- The paired SwiftData stores open through `ModelContainer.openHikes(...)` with the current `OpenHikesSchema`. See *Schema and migration policy* for the reset contract and CloudKit requirements.
- iCloud sync is SwiftData's own CloudKit mirroring, not a sync engine this repo owns. `Hike` lives in a store built with `cloudKitDatabase: .automatic`; everything describing files in *this* device's Application Support lives in `HikeLocalState`, a second `@Model` in a second, unmirrored `ModelConfiguration`. That split is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `TileOwnership` builds its claim set from `offlineDownloads` and `autoSavedTileKeys`, and `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` deletes whatever no hike claims, so mirroring those columns last-writer-wins would strip a second device of tiles it genuinely downloaded. `ModelConfiguration+OpenHikes.swift` is the only place `cloudKitDatabase` is named — build containers through its `ModelContainer.openHikes(...)` factories rather than with a `ModelConfiguration(` literal. Cross-store relationships are illegal, so the two rows join on `hikeID` by value and deleting a hike must call `hike.deleteLocalState()` by hand, *after* any tile-deletion plan has been built from the claim set it is about to remove. A new device-local column belongs in `HikeLocalState` with a passthrough on `Hike`; a new synced column belongs on `Hike` with an inline default. `CloudSyncCoordinator` only reports and toggles: it reads `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.eventChangedNotification`, reduces each event to a `Sendable` `CloudSyncOutcome` on the posting thread, and surfaces `pendingRelaunch` because a `ModelConfiguration` cannot change its mind mid-launch. Letting SwiftData own sync gave four things up deliberately, and none of them is a bug to be found later: photo pixels are files rather than columns and do not travel, so a second device gets a photo's metadata and no file behind it — which the gallery, the map callout and the viewer say in as many words rather than drawing a broken picture, and which is now a decision rather than an open question (see *Settled decisions*); a rename re-uploads the whole row including routes; a recording in progress is a row like any other, so a second device can show a hike whose line is still being drawn; and there is no hook to prefer an unsent local edit over an incoming one. Sync also cannot be exercised between two simulators the way a device pair works — the Simulator receives no CloudKit push, so a second one only picks up changes when it is brought to the foreground.
- **Recording draft cleanup requires positive local ownership.** `Hike.isRecording` is mirrored, but `TrackJournal` is device-local. `HikeLocalState.ownsRecordingDraft` is set only when this device creates a journal or recovers a matching one, saved alongside the draft, and required by the automatic orphan sweep. Tiles, photos and a sidecar row do not establish ownership. An absent journal is never evidence that this device owns a draft; a matching recovered journal can establish ownership.
- Remember only the *negative* entitlement answer. `MapEntitlementStore` persists its resolved answer under `SettingsKey.lastKnownMapEntitlement` and seeds `.notEntitled` at init when that answer was negative, but leaves state `.unknown` when it was positive. The asymmetry is the point: `.unknown` is already permissive, so a subscriber's map never flickers locked on a cold launch before StoreKit answers, while a non-subscriber is never served billed tiles in that window. Seeding the positive too would make a lapsed subscription paint an unlocked map until StoreKit disagreed. The store takes injectable `defaults`; `OpenHikesModel.entitlementDefaults(_:)` hands the app-hosted test bundles a wiped suite so a stub never writes into the developer's real defaults.
- **Following a trail is a walk, and the walk outlives the screen.** `TrailWalkSession`, owned by `OpenHikesModel`, is the one place a walk starts (on the first matched fix in `HikeDetailView.updateLiveFollow`, with Follow This Trail on and never for a recording's draft), accrues (the coverage union in `TrailWalkCoverage` — intervals consecutive matches spanned, never bridged across more than 500 m, so the figure is coverage rather than position), pauses, and ends into a `HikeWalk` row. The walk in progress is a `Codable` column on `HikeLocalState`, device-local like the tile claims and written at milestones and the 45-second publish cadence, never per fix; the finished row is mirrored and hangs off `Hike.walks` with a cascade, and `SheetRoute.walk` is popped with its hike. One walk at a time: while one is active or paused `BackgroundTrailTracker` pins `trackedHikeID` to it and defers selection changes until it ends, so the widget, the Lock Screen and background matching all belong to the walk, and a background relaunch restores it from the sidecar in the model's `init` — before any view — because a fix in a relaunched process has to find the walk it belongs to. Popping the detail, comparing another trail, starting a recording or turning Follow This Trail off changes no walk phase. The toggle controls the live chart position, map pin ownership and permission to auto-start a new walk; enabling it rearms auto-start after an End. An existing walk keeps accruing from both feeds with the toggle off, and keeps its widget and Lock Screen panel. Pause / Resume / End own the walk's manual phase changes, and Resume preserves the toggle's value. Recording is untouched by all of it: the recorder stays the single authority on its draft, the precedence rule below still has exactly three homes, and `TrailWidgetReload.requestUnlessRecording()` still gates the trail feed's redraws. The one `HikeWalk` a walk session does *not* write is the recording's own: `HikeRecorder.persist(_:prepared:customName:)` writes one row per saved recording through `HikeWalk.recorded(_:prepared:)` in `RecordedWalk.swift`, in the same commit that finalizes the draft and rolled back with it if the store refuses, so a recorded hike's History leads with the walk that made it. It carries `TrailWalkEndReason.recorded`, covers the whole route by construction, and is measured against `PreparedRecording.routeLengthMeters` — the plain sum along the saved line, which is what `RouteProfile` measures and therefore the only scale a walk's coverage may be written on; `Hike.distanceMeters` is the hiker's figure, with stationary windows retracted, and a walk written against it would read as a walk along a trail that has since changed. Its active time is `PreparedRecording.recordedSeconds` — the gaps between consecutive saved points, less the leg a pause boundary opened — and **not** wall clock minus `TrackJournalMetadata.pausedIntervals`, which is not a complete record of when a recording was not running: `finishRecovery` parks a recovered session in `.paused` / `.needsDecision` without writing a pause, and no interval exists at all for the stretch between a killed process and the relaunch that finds the journal. It is also the one walk exempt from `TrailWalkPolicy.minimumCoverageMeters`, since a recording the hiker saved is never the glance at a trailhead that rule exists to discard.
- **A reminder is one controller's decision, and its categories are a storage contract.** `MovementReminderController` is handed to the recorder and to the walk session the way `HikeLiveActivityController` is, and for the same reason: *a recording outranks a followed trail* is only expressible by something that can see both, and two controllers would be two banners about one walk. The thresholds live in `MovementReminderPolicy` and nowhere else — five hundred metres from where the pause began, or two hundred and fifty inside two minutes for the bicycle case the issue was raised about, at most three reminders per pause with a quarter of an hour and another crossing between them, and a quarter of an hour of `RecordingDistanceAccumulator.isStationary` before a *running* recording suggests pausing. Displacement from the anchor rather than an accumulated total, because a phone left on a table accumulates half a kilometre of GPS wander and displaces nothing. `MovementReminderKind`'s raw values spell both the notification and the category identifiers, and a delivered notification carries its category for as long as it sits in Notification Centre — so renaming one leaves a hiker holding a banner whose Resume button reaches a delegate that no longer recognises it. The buttons themselves go through `HikeIntentCoordinator`, so a notification action, Siri and the Control Center toggle cannot drift apart; the banner's own tap is left to the system, since routing to a screen is view state a delegate has no way to set. `makeMovementReminderController(defaults:)` returns `nil` under `isRunningTests` rather than `isHostingTests` — UI tests are excluded too, because the authorization prompt is a system alert and a run cannot tap its way past one.
- **A recording always outranks a followed trail**, and one `HikeLiveActivityController` instance is what makes that expressible — the recorder and the tracker are handed the same object. A recording is the thing that would be *lost*; a follow is a convenience the hiker can recreate by selecting the trail again. The controller also owns every rate decision: a 20-second update floor, a 10-second floor on the status flips that bypass it (pausing, losing the trail), stale dates of 10 minutes for a recording and 30 for a follow, and a 5-minute lingering final panel for a *finished* recording only. A discarded recording leaves nothing behind — `end(subject:finalState:dismissAfter:)` treats a `nil` final state as "take it off screen now", and substituting the current state there once silently defeated the discard path. A follow starts only on a *matched* fix, never on mere selection, but keeps updating on an unmatched one so "off the trail" can be said.
- There are no buttons on the Live Activity. The whole panel is a deep-link tap target reusing `TrailWidgetDeepLink`, which lands on the controls that already work; adding a `LiveActivityIntent` remains a separate interaction change rather than part of the Control Center control.
- App Intents run in the app's process but not in its view hierarchy. The system can launch this process purely to perform one, so nothing built by a `.task` or held in the environment is reachable: `OpenHikesApp.init()` registers a `HikeIntentCoordinator` with `AppDependencyManager` and every intent in `OpenHikes/Intents/` is a title, a phrase and one call into it. That coordinator is the *whole* of what an intent can do, and it owns no state — the recorder remains the single authority on whether a hike is being recorded, since the widget, the Live Activity and the recording screen all read it and a fourth answer kept beside them could only ever disagree. It also imports no AppIntents, which is what lets a suite drive start/pause/resume/stop through a real `HikeRecorder` with a stub location source and no ActivityKit, App Group or Core Location behind it. A suite reaches the intents themselves through `HikeIntentContext.$override`, a `@TaskLocal` read in preference to the `@Dependency`: asking `AppDependencyManager` for something never registered traps rather than returning nil, and a plain global would let one test's recorder answer another's intent under parallel execution. The registration is behind the `isRunningTests` guard for the reason the other startup writers are. Recording intents declare `IntentModes.background` — the hiker's hands are busy and the phone is in a pocket — and start and resume add `.foreground(.dynamic)` and *use* it: they `continueInForeground(_:)` when `HikeIntentAuthorization.needsForeground` holds, then carry on in the same `perform()`. Two of Core Location's prompts are foreground-only and the recorder walks into both — `start()` calls `requestWhenInUseAuthorization()` for `.notDetermined`, and `activateSessionIfPossible()` and `resume()` each call `requestTemporaryFullAccuracy()` and then fail with `.preciseLocationRequired` — so `.reducedAccuracy` is reported separately from `.granted` rather than folded into it. `continueInForeground` rather than `needsToContinueInForegroundError`: that error re-*runs* `perform()`, and the re-run would find the same undecided authorization, because nothing between the two runs asked Core Location. The recorder reports refusals by moving to `.failed` rather than by throwing, so an intent that merely awaited `start()` would confirm a hike that never began; `HikeIntentCoordinator` reads the phase back and is where that stays fixed. Every phase-reading entry point awaits `HikeRecorder.settleAutomaticRecovery()` first: a launch that recovers automatically enters `.recovering` *synchronously* in `init`, whether or not there is anything to recover, and the launch these intents exist for is the one the system makes in order to perform one — so an unguarded read answers about the launch ("still finishing your last recording") rather than about the hiker's hike. Everything the coordinator speaks is spoken: `HikeIntentFailure` carries no SwiftData or store diagnostics, which are logged to `OpenHikes`/`Intents` instead, durations go through `HikeFormat.spokenDuration(_:)` rather than the narrow `duration(_:)` a stat tile has room for, a trail match `RecordingStats.isCurrentTrailStale` has overtaken is hedged as "last on" rather than stated, and the finished-hike report reads its clock off the route's own end stamps rather than through `Hike.routeStatistics`, which walks every point on the calling thread — here, the main actor, inside an intent with a system execution budget. `AppShortcutsProvider` is capped at ten shortcuts and drops the rest in silence, which `OpenHikesShortcutsTests` guards.
- The Control Center toggle is the one intent declared in `OpenHikesShared`: the control extension has to compile its action type while the system still performs it in the app's process. It delegates through `HikeRecordingControlHandling`, whose app registration points back to the same `HikeIntentCoordinator`; the shared package never owns a second recording state. Its `StaticControlConfiguration` projects the App Group recording payload to start/stop, and `RecordingSharedStateStore` reloads that control alongside the widget timeline whenever the payload changes. The toggle is the one entry point that reads `HikeRecorder.phase` itself before delegating, so it settles automatic recovery first for the reason the rest of the coordinator does — and more sharply, since a Control Center tap is the likeliest of all to launch the process purely to perform an intent. It takes the same two foreground-only prompts as seriously as start and resume do: it reports `requiresForegroundAuthorization` when `HikeIntentAuthorization.needsForeground` holds, and the intent then `continueInForeground(_:)`s and calls back with `canPromptForLocation: true` — a re-run through `needsToContinueInForegroundError` would find the same unanswered authorization, because nothing between the two runs asked Core Location. This build proves App Intents metadata extraction from the shared package for both products, but it does not add or validate a `LiveActivityIntent`.
- Keep persisted identifiers stable: provider IDs, `SettingsKey` strings, `CloudSyncCoordinator.containerIdentifier`, `SharedStore.appGroupID`, widget kind, cache-key shape, and deep-link format are shared across launches, devices or targets. Update all entitlements/consumers together if an App Group or CloudKit container contract changes. CloudKit schema changes follow *Schema and migration policy*.
- Both unit-test bundles are hosted by the app, so it launches and runs its `.task`s before any test does. Startup work that writes shared state — today `OpenHikesView.restoreLastSelectedHike()`, which publishes a widget payload — must stay behind the `isRunningTests` guard, or it races the suites that assert on that state. The same guard is what keeps the test host from mirroring to the developer's real iCloud account, since it builds its own container at launch. UI tests run out-of-process and identify the app-under-test with `--ui-testing`. `Fixture.hike(in:configure:)` inserts before it runs `configure`, and must keep doing so: `Hike`'s device-local passthroughs are a silent no-op on a row with no `modelContext`.
- The app ships for iPhone only: every target declares `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "iphoneos iphonesimulator"` and `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = 1`. An embedded extension's device family has to stay a subset of its host's, so `OpenWidget` moves with the app rather than independently. The `canImport(UIKit)`/`canImport(AppKit)` aliases and `#if os(iOS)` guards in the existing sources are kept — they cost nothing and are what a later iPad, Mac or visionOS target would be rebuilt from — but nothing verifies those paths compile any more, so treat them as unbuilt rather than supported.
- A composite row is one accessibility element, not four. `HikeRow`, `StatTile`, `DetailRow` and the settings rows hide their decoration and expose a single label/value pair, so a UI test locates a row by its identifier plus a label prefix (`hikeRow(titled:)` in `UITestSupport.swift`) rather than by the `staticTexts` inside it. Selection that is drawn only as a tint or a checkmark also carries `.isSelected`; a glyph-only button carries its own `accessibilityLabel` and a `minimumTapTarget()`. Anything decorative is `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, and a `Text` that interpolates an SF Symbol needs a spoken label beside it. An identifier on a container is worse than none: SwiftUI pushes it down onto every descendant, so it both smothers the leaf identifiers underneath it and makes a whole section answer to one name — which is why the surface and difficulty sections carry theirs on the bar alone. `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are what enforce this.
- `OpenHikes/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` is part of the shipping contract, not documentation. It declares four required-reason API codes — `CA92.1` for the app's own `UserDefaults`, `C617.1` and `3B52.1` for file timestamps inside the app's containers and through the document picker, and `35F9.1` for system uptime used as an elapsed-time measurement — plus `NSPrivacyTracking: false` and empty collected-data and tracking-domain arrays. An upload without it is rejected with ITMS-91053, and the rejection names the API rather than the manifest, so reaching for a new required-reason API means adding its code here in the same change. `OpenHikes/` is a file-system-synchronized group whose only membership exception is `Info.plist`, so the manifest is bundled with no `project.pbxproj` edit. Apple's authoritative code list is the DocC JSON behind `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons`; the rendered HTML page is JavaScript-only and cannot be read by a fetch. `OpenWidgetExtension` deliberately carries **no** manifest of its own: it was audited and calls none of the required-reason APIs — `SharedStore` enumerates with `includingPropertiesForKeys: nil` and reads no timestamp, and the widget touches no `UserDefaults` and no uptime — so a manifest there would declare reasons the binary does not use. If a future upload rejection names the extension, that audit is what changed.
- `Info.plist` declares `NSSupportsLiveActivities`, without which `Activity.request` throws and nothing appears — the failure is silent from the hiker's side. `NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates` is deliberately *absent*: this app updates on the hiker's own movement at a 20-second floor, which is well inside the ordinary budget, and asking for the frequent-update allowance would trade a battery warning in Settings for a rate nothing here wants. The hiker's own switch is `SettingsKey.liveActivitiesEnabled`, on by default; the system's per-app switch is read separately through `areActivitiesEnabled`, and both have to say yes.
- Never commit `OpenHikes/Secrets.plist`. Copy `Secrets.example.plist` locally for Stadia or Thunderforest keys; OpenStreetMap remains the keyless default.

## Schema and migration policy

The app currently has one installed device, its existing data is disposable, and the developer can reset local data and manage the CloudKit database. Preserve only the current formats. Do not add frozen historical models, `SchemaMigrationPlan` stages, launch-time data conversions, legacy decoding branches or fields retained solely for compatibility while these assumptions hold. This is a development reset policy, not a promise that an older store will open. Do not automatically erase stores on an open failure: the existing in-memory fallback and startup alert still handle corruption and I/O failures.

`OpenHikesSchema` is the single SwiftData schema, starting at version `1.0.0` for this fresh-store baseline and using the live `Hike`, `HikeWalk` and `HikeLocalState` types. Both production and disk-backed test factories use it without a migration plan. Edit the live shape directly during this phase. This version starts a new baseline after discarding the previous stores; it neither reuses the historical V1 model nor downgrades an existing store or the CloudKit schema. Renumbering is acceptable only while previous stores are explicitly unsupported and reset. Old schemas and conversion implementations belong in git history. Keep current-format persistence tests that reopen both stores, verify the `hikeID` join and exercise deletion and recording recovery.

For an incompatible change, stop the app and widget and discard the affected local state before running the new build: both SwiftData stores and their SQLite side files/external storage, device-local tile manifests and files, recording journals, App Group snapshots/basemaps/pending fixes, or persisted settings as applicable. A clean reinstall plus clearing the shared App Group state is the simplest full reset. Coordinate any mirrored-data reset with the local reset so old cloud records cannot repopulate the fresh store. Clearing only the cloud database does not repair a local store, and clearing only local data can download the old cloud records again. This cleanup changes no mirrored fields and performs no live reset; pre-cleanup local stores and tile manifests are unsupported.

CloudKit still imposes its own constraints: non-optional mirrored attributes need inline defaults, relationships must be optional, and uniqueness constraints are forbidden. Keep the mirrored and unmirrored configurations separate: tile files, photo pixels and recording journals are still device-local, including after reinstalling or restoring cloud data on the same device. The tests in `MirroredCloudKitSchemaTests` check these constraints and compare the current mirrored fields against `MirroredCloudKitSchema.recordTypes`; they do not contact CloudKit.

CloudKit **records and schema are different**. The developer may clear disposable records, but resetting development restores the production schema if one exists; promoted record types and fields cannot simply be deleted, renamed or retyped. Use compatible additions or a new container if an incompatible production shape is unavoidable. Before a build uses the production environment, verify and deploy the current development schema in CloudKit Console, including every mirrored record type and field (`CD_Hike`, `CD_HikeWalk` and their `CD_` fields). No production deployment has been recorded in this repository as of 2026-09-09; that is not verification of the Console's current state. Record verified deployment/reset facts here, not in runtime code or a date-parsing test. Apple's [model constraints](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coredata/creating-a-core-data-model-for-cloudkit) and [schema deployment guidance](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/deploying-an-icloud-container-s-schema) own the platform rules.

The app and widget keep explicit current-format versions for their shared snapshots (currently v1). A version is required and only an exact match is read; missing, older, newer and malformed versions are refused with diagnostics. There is no unversioned-v0 fallback or rewrite-on-save upgrade. Keep this format check and the journal header/version check: rejecting unreadable bytes is ordinary validation, not a migration. Optional fields remain optional when absence has a current meaning, such as no walk, no elevation or no custom name. Derived caches can be regenerated when their current shape fails to decode.

Tile keys contain provider/zoom/x/y only. No provider substitutes display scale into its URL, so the former scale suffix split identical tiles between renderer and downloader. The scale suffix converter, file renamer and unused `OfflineDownloadRecord.scale` are removed; reset old tile state instead. Weather readings require their explicit subject kind. Do not retain old payload acceptance tests as current requirements. Recording flag bit 1 is unused; the current bit values remain unchanged without carrying retired-journal compatibility tests.

Revisit this policy only when installs or data must survive upgrades. At that point, freeze the actual then-current model and every encoded value type before changing it, introduce a real versioned migration plan, and test on-disk previous-version stores through both configurations. Recover historical shapes from git if they truly need support; never invent a previous schema by putting a new version number on today's model. Keep any future migration rationale, reset procedure and CloudKit deployment notes in this section rather than scattering them through source headers, README or separate migration documents.

## Render isolation, in practice

The claim these rules protect is measured rather than asserted: an idle app with a map on screen evaluates zero SwiftUI bodies and costs 0.6% of one core, a sustained chart scrub moves the map seventeen times without re-evaluating any body above the chart, and a backgrounded recording renders nothing at all. A run's own report carries the figures. Five rules below each produced a convincing wrong answer first, and are worth knowing before changing anything on the render path.

**Only a `View` type is a boundary.** A helper `func`, a computed `var`, and a `.toolbar`/`.safeAreaInset`/`.overlay` closure are all inlined into the body that declares them, so an observable read inside one registers as an input of *that* body. This is how a tick mark came to rebuild a whole photo grid: the selection lived correctly in an `@Observable` controller, and the cells were built by a `private func cell(_:at:)` in the sheet's scope. If a body is re-running and the observable read is not visible in it, look for those four before looking anywhere else.

**State can be correctly owned and incorrectly placed.** `@State` invalidates its declaring view whether or not `body` reads it — a navigation path held as `@State` on the root re-rendered the entire map screen underneath a full-screen cover that completely obscured it, and an `.onChange` writing a `@State` that no body ever read still cost two body evaluations. `SheetPresentation` is the fix shape: a stable `@Observable` holding the raw state as `@ObservationIgnored` storage and publishing only coarser derived flags, so pushing a photo onto a hike — the same screen at the same height — flips nothing at all.

**`@Environment(\.dismiss)` is the dynamic property that invalidates most.** The rule above is not about `@State` in particular: *any* `DynamicProperty` invalidates its declaring view whether or not `body` reads it, and `DismissAction` is the one that changes constantly. SwiftUI hands out a fresh, non-equatable one on every pass through the presentation machinery, and a single scene-phase transition drives several — so `Button("Done") { dismiss() }` written into a screen's own `.toolbar` re-renders that whole screen every time the app leaves or re-enters the foreground, for a value nothing on screen depends on. Measured on the `photo-discovery` scenario: one backgrounding rebuilt the twelve-cell review grid, its toolbar and every cell's accessibility label **eight** times across ~300 ms, and SwiftUI's own `_logChanges()` named `_dismiss` as the only changed property in seven of the eight. The same shape cost `HikePhotoViewer` seven passes of a screen that re-sorts the gallery on each, and `SettingsView` six of a seven-section `Form`. `DismissButton` and `.dismiss(when:)` in `General/Dismissal.swift` are the fix shape, and they work because a `ViewModifier` is a boundary for the same reason a `View` is: its dynamic properties are its own, and its `body(content:)` re-wraps a subtree the parent has already built. No screen should declare `@Environment(\.dismiss)` when the only thing that closes it is a button or a condition.

**A computed property that sorts looks like a field access.** `Hike.orderedPhotos` was read six times in one body pass of the photo viewer for that reason. Its comparator also allocated: comparing `(capturedAt, id.uuidString)` tuples makes Swift build both sides before comparing, so every comparison allocated two 36-character strings rather than only the ties the tie-break exists for.

**Not every well-argued prediction survives a measurement.** `SettingsView`'s unbounded `@Query` was predicted to charge all seven `Form` sections for every write to any `Hike`. Measured, it was 2.0 body evaluations either way, because SwiftData coalesces the writes into one invalidation the explicit state changes already paid for. A prediction about SwiftUI cost is a hypothesis; measure both sides.

**A same-value write is filtered by `@Observable`, not by SwiftData — and only when the type is `Equatable`.** Measured across `String`, `Double`, `Bool`, `Date`, `UUID`, `String?`, dictionaries, an `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` array and a to-many relationship: a `@Model` notifies on **every** write, equal or not, inserted into a context or not, and does so per-property. A plain `@Observable` storing an `Equatable` value notifies on **none** of them; storing a non-`Equatable` one — `CLLocationCoordinate2D` — notifies on all. The filtering lives in `@Observable`'s macro expansion. Three consequences. A dedup guard on an `Equatable` `@Observable` property (`RouteStyle.apply`, `SheetPresentation.pathDidChange`) is belt-and-braces over undocumented runtime behaviour and **cannot be protected by a zero-assertion test** — delete it and the test stays green, because the runtime already filtered the write. A dedup guard on a non-`Equatable` one (`RouteHighlight.move(to:)`, `LocationManager.publish`) is load-bearing app code and its test really does go red. And a test asserting a zero *upstream* of an `@Observable` needs an explicit precondition that the write it is filtering actually happened, or it measures nothing. `OpenHikesTests/Map/RenderIsolationTests+Observation.swift` pins both runtime behaviours; those pins are the tripwire if either changes, and they are the one thing in that family that cannot be mutation-verified, since a runtime change cannot be induced.

**A zero-assertion is only evidence if you have watched it go red.** Around thirty in the render-isolation family were audited by deleting the behaviour each claimed to hold; two were decorative for the reason above, and one hole was real and unrelated — `LocationManager.minimumPublishInterval` could be deleted entirely with the whole suite still green, because `ObservationCounter` re-arms through a `Task` and so sees ten writes in one runloop turn exactly once either way. An observation count cannot measure a throttle; assert the throttle's observable effect instead.

Use `RenderSignpost` and the `RENDER_SIGNPOST_LOG=1` scheme variable when changing this flow, and add a mark for any new work placed on the path — `Purchases/` and the widget's timeline provider carry none today, which is precisely why a rendering problem in either would be invisible to the performance suite.

## Maintaining the performance harness

Every rule here produced a convincing wrong answer first, and each one is a way for `PerformanceUITests` to report a number that is about the harness rather than the app.

**The observer perturbs the observed.** The first interaction with a newly-presented screen forces XCUITest to hit-test against a hierarchy it has not described before, and SwiftUI evaluates bodies to answer — charged to the gesture, this made one chart scrub report 2 and 5 on consecutive runs of identical code. `warmAccessibilityTree(around:in:)` pays that cost before the baseline reading, but it performs a real centre tap and so has to be *aimed*: warming on the photo strip navigates into the viewer, and warming on the Settings form's centre lands on the tile-provider list and either switches the map source or opens the paywall. Warm on a harmless control on the same screen, after scrolling it into view.

**A fixed settle time cannot be both correct and fast.** `settle(in:)` polls the app's own counters and returns once nothing has re-rendered for 1.5 s, ignoring the sampler's entries — which tick every second regardless and would otherwise mean the app never looked quiet. A new counter that ticks on a timer **must** be added to the `sampled` exclusion set in `PerformanceCounters.isEquivalent(to:)`, or every recording scenario spins to its timeout.
