**A suite made entirely of upper bounds cannot notice work that has stopped.** Instrumenting the 1 Hz clock nearly broke it: extracting the readout into a view that stored the *recorder* made the view structurally identical on every tick, so SwiftUI skipped its body and the clock silently froze — scoring perfectly against every budget in the suite. The view now stores the formatted string, so what SwiftUI diffs is the thing on screen, and `RecordingClockTick` carries a *lower* bound in the foreground scenario as well as an upper bound in the backgrounded one. Any counter measuring work that is supposed to happen needs the same pair.

**A cache is a lie detector that has already been bribed.** The offline scenario asserts that browsing opens no connection, and on its first run it passed instantly and proved nothing — every tile in the region was already on disk from the previous scenario, so there was no miss and no fetch to refuse. `--ui-test-offline` hands the launch an empty tile root for this reason, which turned 0 refusals into 45.

**A permission dialog must not decide whether you get data.** The recording scenario once reset location authorization and relied on a UI interruption monitor to answer the alert; when that failed, Core Location delivered nothing and the run produced fifty-one seconds of an idle app, which looks like a measurement but is the absence of one. `Scripts/run-performance-tests.sh` grants the permission out-of-band with `simctl privacy`, and the monitor stays only as a fallback.

**A harness failure will happily impersonate a product failure.** Four runs back to back once produced a different failure each time — `kAXErrorServerNotFound`, `Error getting main window`, `Application … is not running` — and never the same test twice. None were assertions; all were the accessibility server being asked about an app that had not finished coming forward, because both `launch()` and `activate()` return before the state they name is true. `bringToForeground(_:)` blocks on `XCUIApplication.wait(for: .runningForeground)` first. When a performance suite starts failing *differently* on each run, suspect the harness.

**A test the runner cannot find is a test that passes.** `run-performance-tests.sh` once built its list by scanning `PerformanceUITests.swift` alone, after the suite had grown into `+Photos.swift` and `+Screens.swift`, so `--list` under-reported and `--test` rejected names that existed. It scans `PerformanceUITests*.swift` now. Anything that decides *which* tests run is part of the harness and needs the same suspicion as the assertions, which is what `Scripts/run-script-tests.sh` covers: it runs both simulator-driving scripts against a stubbed `xcrun` and `xcodebuild` and asserts the device each command addressed, that a run collecting no scenario logs fails rather than reporting success, and that a scenario log a previous run left in the app container is cleared before the run rather than copied out and reported as this one's. It covers `lint.sh` against a stubbed `swiftlint` for the same reason — a lint that accepted an option it did not understand reports "clean" about a run it never configured as asked. It covers `perf-report.py` for the same reason again, against a fixture rather than a stub: the findings list is what a person reads first after a performance run, and a finding about the instrument — the sampler's own counter, the scene transition a phase pays at its edges, an interval deliberately kept off the main thread, a tile fetched as the app comes back onto the screen — reads exactly like a regression until somebody checks it against the event file by hand.

**A synthesised tap is briefer than any real one, and a gesture with a press threshold reads as dead to it.** `XCUICoordinate.tap()` puts a finger down and lifts it in essentially no time, where a person's quickest tap still lasts tens of milliseconds. Swift Charts' own `.chartXSelection` gesture resolves nothing until a *stationary* touch has lasted about a tenth of a second — measured on iOS 26.5 as between 0.08 s and 0.10 s, with a touch that moves engaging it at once — so the `chart-scrub` phase read **zero** `ElevationChartBody` evaluations against 25 for a drag over the same pixels, and #206 was filed as "a tap on the elevation chart scrubs nothing" with three candidate causes, all of them wrong. The counter was right and the conclusion drawn from it was twice too strong: the threshold was real, but it was a threshold rather than the absence of a gesture. Settling it took eight `press(forDuration:)` probes either side of the boundary. A phase whose gesture may not have arrived needs an `assertAtLeast` saying it did — a suite of upper bounds scores a dead gesture perfectly — and a zero that is *interesting* deserves a probe before it becomes an issue.

**A ratio can invent a finding.** The report generator once flagged a backgrounded recording for "52.2 network requests per accepted fix", which was arithmetic rather than a fact: it charged the tiles the foreground map loaded at launch against the three fixes a short scenario accepts. That scenario in fact woke the radio zero times. The generator counts requests inside the backgrounded windows now, and every ratio it draws a conclusion from — bodies per accepted fix, requests per backgrounded window, rejections per fix that reached the recorder — is asserted in `Scripts/tests/` against input small enough to check by hand. `Scripts/run-script-tests.sh` still runs the whole generator against a fixture, which is the half that catches a findings list assembled wrongly out of arithmetic that is individually right.

There is no canonical list of signpost names, and any list written into a document would drift: `RenderSignpost` takes a `StaticString`, so a name exists only at its call site. Read them off the code instead — `rg -o --no-filename 'RenderSignpost\.\w+\(\s*"[A-Za-z]+"' --glob '*.swift' | sed -E 's/.*"([A-Za-z]+)".*/\1/' | sort -u`. The prefixes worth knowing are `…Body` for a SwiftUI body evaluation, `Map…` for anything reaching `MKMapView`, `Recording…`/`Live…` for the fix pipeline — with `LiveActivity…` the exception, which is the Lock Screen panel rather than a fix —, `Photo…` for decode and ordering, `Tile…`/`Offline…` for storage and download, and `AppModelInit`/`ModelContainerInit`/`GPXParsed`/`HikeTrailAnalysis` for startup and I/O intervals.

`General/Diagnostics/FieldMetrics/` is the MetricKit half, and note it is *not* `#if DEBUG` — unlike everything else in `Diagnostics/` — because MetricKit only delivers against Release builds in the field. It is split along one line: `FieldMetricsDigest.swift` holds every judgement the app makes about a payload and imports no MetricKit at all, which is the only reason `FieldMetricsDigestTests` can exist, since `MXMetricPayload` has no initializer and cannot be synthesised. Only four `mxSignpost` spans exist, deliberately: Apple limits how many the system processes and the failure mode is silent, so a fifth span does not error, it costs the other four their data. `FieldSignpost.Span` is `CaseIterable` and its count is asserted, so a fifth has to be added on purpose.

## Energy policies in force

Five policies decide what the app spends. Each was a measured finding once and each is now shipping behaviour, with the full argument in the source header so the rationale cannot drift away from the code it justifies. Do not weaken one without a measurement.

- **GPS accuracy is a function of conditions**, not a constant (`Recording/RecordingEnergyPolicy.swift`). `desiredAccuracy` drops only for Low Power Mode or thermal `.serious` and above; `distanceFilter` widens for those and for standing still, taking the larger candidate. `.fair` thermal is deliberately excluded — a phone in a sunlit jacket pocket sits there all summer, and a mitigation that is always on is indistinguishable from having lowered the default. `PowerStateMonitor` watches both notifications, so the transition with no fix to prompt it — a hiker stopping for lunch as the battery crosses 20% — still reconfigures.
- **Tile fetching is split by purpose**, not by caller (`Tiles/TileNetworkPolicy.swift`). What matters is whether anyone is waiting for the tile: `loadTile` takes the purpose and defaults to `.interactive`, while `saveTileDurably` fixes it at `.speculative`. Cellular allows interactive and denies speculative; offline and Low Data Mode deny both; Low Power Mode and thermal pressure deny only speculative. The asymmetry is the point — a hiker looking at the map gets their tile, and what stops is the app spending a metered radio on tiles nobody asked to see. None of it is configurable, because a switch is a question the hiker has to answer correctly *before* the walk to get the right behaviour during it. Every refusal emits `TileFetchSuppressed` with `purpose=` and `reason=`; a tile that silently never loads is the hardest thing in this pipeline to debug, and this policy creates that situation on purpose.
- **A pause spends nothing unless something will read it** (`Reminders/MovementReminderController.swift`, `RecordingLocationSource.startMovementWatch()`). `HikeRecorder.pause()` used to stop the GPS outright; it now asks the reminder controller whether the pause is worth watching and stops it outright whenever the answer is no — reminders switched off, or a pause taken before the first fix, which leaves no anchor to measure a departure from. When the answer is yes the watch is the *cheapest delivery that can still notice a departure*, and which one that is depends on authorization rather than on a setting: Always gets significant-location-change monitoring, which needs neither the background mode nor the activity session, so the continuous feed, the session and the status indicator all go for the length of the pause; When In Use keeps the feed at `RecordingEnergyProfile.pausedWatch` (hundred-metre accuracy, hundred-metre filter), because an app that stops updating location is suspended and a suspended app notices nothing at all. A paused *walk* along a followed trail is watched by the matched fixes its feeds were already delivering and costs nothing new — which also means it is silent for a hiker whose phone is in a pocket with background tracking off, and the settings footer gives that case its own sentence — a paused walk is watched while the app is open, and behind it only with Background Trail Tracking on — rather than letting the recording's “without Always access” clause stand for both and promising a reminder the app cannot send.
- **The display is held only on a claim, and only if asked** (`General/ScreenWake.swift`). `isIdleTimerDisabled` was never set, which is right for a six-hour walk in a pocket and wrong for a hiker standing at a junction while the screen dims every thirty seconds — each of those wakes pays a display ramp and a render, repeatedly, so the cheap default is the expensive one in exactly the case it was meant to help. So it is a switch, `SettingsKey.keepScreenAwake`, **off** by default, and three answers have to agree before anything is held: the switch, a *live* subject (a recording session that exists, or a walk under way), and `scenePhase == .active`. It is scoped to the two screens where the question arises — `RecordingView` and `HikeDetailView` — through `.keepsScreenAwake(while:)`, so a Settings screen left open in a pocket holds nothing. `ScreenWakeCoordinator` counts claims rather than storing a flag, because a navigation transition presents the incoming screen before the outgoing one disappears and a flag would be cleared by the screen that was leaving; it is also the one place `UIApplication.isIdleTimerDisabled` is written, behind an injectable seam, since both unit bundles are hosted by the app.
- **A backgrounded recording draws nothing and ticks nothing.** `MapView.Coordinator` gates the overlay apply on foreground, observed through `UIApplication` lifecycle notifications rather than `scenePhase` so it stays entirely off SwiftUI's render path; the `withObservationTracking` registration continues regardless, since the revision must keep being tracked, and the work is deferred rather than dropped and caught up in one pass on return. `RecordingHeader` builds its 1 Hz `TimelineView` only while `scenePhase` is `.active` — that one *is* on the render path, deliberately, because the question is whether the `TimelineView` is in the hierarchy at all and only SwiftUI can answer it. Do not assume iOS suspends that timer: a suspended app runs no timers, but this app holds the location background mode for the entire hike, which is exactly what keeps it running.

## The community feature

Sharing a hike publishes it to the **public** CloudKit database of the same container the mirrored store uses. That is a different database with a different owner: public storage is the developer's, private storage is the hiker's own iCloud quota. The distinction is what makes this feature possible at all without contradicting *Photo pixels stay on the device the photo was added on* below — that decision is about the private database and still holds.

**Every submission is reviewed by a person, and the gate is the schema rather than a flag.** CloudKit grants permissions per *record type*, never per field or per record. A single type with a `moderationState` field therefore cannot express this: whoever may write a submission may write whatever they like into their own state field. So there are two types, and `CommunitySchema` is the one place they are spelled:

- `CommunityHikeSubmission` — what a hiker uploads. `_world` read, `_icloud` create, `_creator` **read only**. Anybody may make one; nobody but the reviewer may change one.
- `CommunityHike` — the published listing, carrying a reference to a submission plus the denormalised fields a query needs. `_world` read, and create *and write* granted to a custom admin role and to nobody else. One of those fields is `authorID`, the submission's creator, which the reviewer copies across from the submission's *Created By* when they publish — see *Blocking is device-local* below for what it is for and why a listing without it is dropped.

Publishing is therefore creating one `CommunityHike` record by hand in the CloudKit Console, which is what lets review ship before any review tooling does. No build of this app can create one; `CommunityTransporting` has no method for it, deliberately.

**A submission is write-once, and that is what makes review mean anything.** The listing points at the submission rather than at a copy of its contents, so an author who kept write access could swap the route, the description or the photo assets of an already-approved submission and have `detail(for:)` serve the replacement under the approved listing, unreviewed. Hence no write permission outside the admin role — which also means the app cannot withdraw or amend a submission: sharing an amended hike makes a new one, and a takedown is a reviewer's delete. `_world` reads the type for the other half of the same fetch: a reference being readable does not make its target readable, and browsing is account-free, so without it a signed-out hiker could find a hike and not open it. The cost, stated plainly: an unreviewed submission is readable by anyone holding its record name — unguessable, and not enumerable, but a name rather than a permission. The alternative, copying every approved route and photograph into an admin-only record, cannot be done by hand in the Console for a dozen assets and would make review wait on tooling that does not exist yet.

**Indexes are not created by a first save, and a query against an unindexed field fails at runtime.** On `CommunityHike` the Console needs `location` QUERYABLE *and* SORTABLE (the predicate filters on it and the results sort by distance from the same point), `title` SEARCHABLE (the typed query is a full-text `self contains`, because CloudKit's `BEGINSWITH` is case-sensitive and anchored), and `publishedAt` SORTABLE. `authorID` needs **no index**: blocking is applied on the device, so the field is read off rows that have already arrived and is never a predicate — indexing it would let anybody enumerate one person's published hikes. On `CommunityHikeSubmission`, **no index at all** — including the `___recordID` QUERYABLE the Console adds by default, which has to be removed. `routeOutline`, added to that type for the map's lines, is no exception and needs none: it is read by a fetch of record IDs with `desiredKeys`, which is a fetch and not a query. That absence is the security control that keeps a world-readable pending submission from being enumerable: the type is only ever *fetched by record ID*, which needs no index, and adding one would list every unreviewed upload to anybody. **Deployed to the development environment on 2026-09-12 and verified there**, with `xcrun cktool import-schema` rather than by hand in the Console — export the schema, edit that file, import it back, because the import is declarative and whole-file. `CommunityHikeSubmission.routeOutline` postdates that import and **reached development on its own, carrying `QUERYABLE SEARCHABLE SORTABLE`** — the auto-created defaults the paragraph below warns about, and the enumeration leak this whole rule exists to refuse. It has to be stripped by another import; see *Still missing before this can ship*. That is the warning demonstrating itself within a day of being written, so read it as a standing instruction rather than a historical note: **re-export after every change and look at the index list, because the field you just added is indexed**. The custom role is called `reviewer` and was created by `CREATE ROLE reviewer;` in the same file; no Console step was needed for it. Two things the live container taught: a type CloudKit auto-creates from a first save arrives with `GRANT WRITE TO "_creator"` and every field QUERYABLE, SEARCHABLE and SORTABLE, which is how `CommunityHikeSubmission` first existed here — pending submissions were enumerable in practice, not in theory, until the import above replaced it; and a field added to `CommunitySchema` later will reach the database with those same defaults, so re-export and re-check after any change rather than assuming this shape held. **Production is deployed, in the shape that predates all of this, and that is worse than not being deployed.** `cktool` has no promote subcommand and cannot even validate against production (`endpoint not applicable in the environment 'production'`), so the promote stays a Console button and the only way to read production is `export-schema --environment production`. Do that before believing anything in this paragraph. As of 2026-09-12 it holds `CD_Hike`, `CD_HikeWalk` and a `CommunityHikeSubmission` that is the **auto-created** shape: every field QUERYABLE, SEARCHABLE and SORTABLE, and `GRANT WRITE TO "_creator"`. Both halves of the schema's reason for existing are therefore absent in production — an author can rewrite their own approved submission, and pending submissions are enumerable. It is not reachable today, because production has no `CommunityHike` record type and no `reviewer` role, so nothing can be published or browsed there and no shipped build points at it. It is what a deploy would be correcting rather than creating, and nothing here has established that a deploy *can* drop an index or downgrade a `GRANT` in production. Check that it did, afterwards. Two things block the press besides the index above: `CD_Hike` in **development** is missing `author`, `importedAuthorName`, `keywords` and `trackDescription`, all four stored `String?` on the model and none ever exported with a non-nil value, so SwiftData has never created the columns — promote now and the first hiker to type a description has their export silently rejected. See issue #205, and note that `MirroredCloudKitSchemaTests` did not catch that four-field gap.

**The map's results and the typed query's are separate lists.** `CommunityBrowser` keeps `nearbyListings` and `matchingListings` apart, with one in-flight task each, because they answer different questions and are drawn in different places — the *Community Hikes* section of the hikes list (and, while typing, a *Near Here* section under the matches) and the *Community Hikes* search section. While they shared one array a pan past the policy's threshold overwrote a typed search's results, and clearing the field left title matches standing wherever the zoom ceiling refused the replacement query. `state` describes the nearby request alone; a failed title search is logged and touches neither it nor the remembered region. The search field coalesces title edits through a cancellable `.task(id:)` and a 300 ms clock wait, keyed by the trimmed, lowercased query. Edits cancel the old title response synchronously; clearing also drops matches immediately, and Return submits the pending query without waiting or asking twice. That deduplication is about reusing an *answer*, so a failed title search forgets the word it asked and Return can ask it again — nothing on screen reports a failed title search, which makes resubmitting the only retry there is. This bounds requests during typing; no battery saving has been measured.

**The map offers, and the hiker asks.** `distanceToLocation:` resolves at around ten kilometres, so a request per pan spends the shared public-database quota redrawing an identical list. `CommunityQueryPolicy` therefore refuses unless the centre moved more than a quarter of the last radius or the zoom changed by more than a factor of two, and answers `.tooFarOut` above a 150 km radius, where a result means "somewhere on this continent". What it returns is an **offer** rather than a search: `action(for:)` is side-effect free — a pan is a run of settles and the second must not withdraw what the first raised — `CommunityBrowser.areaPrompt` is what the map draws as *Search this area*, and `commit(_:)` records the area only when the hiker takes it. That is both cheaper than the automatic re-query it replaced (a pan nobody confirms costs nothing) and the only version of this that is legible: the list used to replace itself under the hiker's thumb for reasons nothing on screen gave. `CommunityAreaName` then heads the list with the place MapKit calls that area, so *Nearby* is a description rather than a control. Browsing is still opt-in — until the *Find community hikes near here* row is tapped nothing reaches the network, geocoder included — and that one tap is the single request nobody confirms twice. The region reaches `CommunityBrowser` from `MapView.Coordinator`'s `regionDidChangeAnimated` and is stored `@ObservationIgnored`, so no SwiftUI body reads it.

**The shared hikes are a section of the hiker's own list, and they are on the map.** The *Nearby* chip used to replace the hikes list wholesale, which made one question — where shall I walk? — into two screens that had to be chosen between, and put the same records under two headings depending on how they were found. They are one list now, with *Community Hikes* beneath the hiker's own and a *Hide* button in its header where the chip's off switch went. The results are also drawn as `MKMarkerAnnotationView`s through `MapCommunityAnnotations`, which closes the loop the feature was missing: the region is the query and, until then, its answer existed only as rows in a sheet drawn over the map that asked. The pins are observed off `nearbyListings` by the coordinator and a callout's accessory opens the same preview a row does, through `CommunityBrowser.onOpenListing` — set by `OpenHikesView`, because MapKit draws the pins and the destination is a push into a stack the map cannot see. Both the pill and the pins are UIKit for the reason the camera pill is: a SwiftUI overlay reading `areaPrompt` would put every offer and withdrawal through the root view's body.

**And they are lines, not only points, before anything is imported.** A trail is a line before it is a place, and a marker on a trailhead says nothing about whether the walk behind it climbs the ridge or follows the valley — so `MapCommunityRoutes` draws every hike in the answer, at half strength and at `.aboveRoads`, below the level the hiker's own route is added at. Where the two cross, theirs wins; the tint is the app's rather than `RouteStyle`'s, for the reason the markers' is. The pins stay alongside and that is not caution: a polyline is not an accessibility element and cannot be one, so VoiceOver reaches a shared hike through its marker, and markers declutter where lines cannot. MapKit hit-tests annotations and never overlays, so the tap is this app's own — a recognizer installed in `makeMapView`, `CommunityRouteHitTest` for the geometry, and `Coordinator.communityListing(forTapAt:in:)` as the seam between them, because a `UITapGestureRecognizer`'s state and location are set by the touch system and cannot be driven by a suite. The pick is *nearest within a fingertip* rather than first: two trails sharing a valley floor overlap at any zoom showing both. The measurement is in screen points, deliberately — the tolerance is a distance on the glass, and in map points the same number would mean forty metres at one zoom and four kilometres at another.

**The geometry that makes that affordable is a separate, thinner copy of the route.** `CommunityListing` still carries none: a page is twenty-five of them and twenty-five recorded routes is tens of megabytes for a list the hiker may scroll straight past, which is why the browse path fetched no route at all. `CommunityRouteOutline` is the middle term — the same line thinned by Ramer–Douglas–Peucker to at most 128 points and encoded as a Google polyline, about a kilobyte, so a whole page is about twenty-five. It is a **field** on `CommunityHikeSubmission` where the route is an asset, and that is the whole of why it earns its place: a field can be asked for by itself, so `CommunityTransporting.outlines(for:)` fetches the lot in one `records(for:desiredKeys:)` and nothing else comes with it. It therefore needs **no index** and must not be given one — it is read by a fetch of record IDs taken off published listings, which is the only way that type is ever read, and the absence of any index on it is the control that keeps submissions unenumerable. It is also **not** denormalised onto the listing: that would spend a hand-typed field in the Console on every publication for a round trip nobody is waiting on. Nothing computes a statistic from an outline and nothing imports one — elevation, timestamps, provenance and pause boundaries are all gone and the points have moved by up to the tolerance — and `CommunityRouteOutline.decoded(_:)` is strict to the point of refusing the whole line, because what it reads is text off a public record that a person may have pasted by hand: a truncated paste, an unpaired value or a coordinate off the planet draws nothing at all rather than a route through the Atlantic. The fetch is its own task off `accept(_:answering:about:)`, counted in `requestsInFlight` and deliberately not in `issuedRequests` — one answer is one question however many requests carry it back — and a failure costs the lines and nothing else, because the rows and pins are already up. An absent outline is the ordinary case, not an error: every hike published before the field existed has none, and those keep their pin and draw no line.

**The preview's route is on the map, and the preview's numbers are on the preview.** `CommunityHikeView` used to draw the route itself, as an unscaled sketch with no ground under it, on a screen presented over a real map that was drawing the same trail as a single pin. Both halves have moved. The screen tells `CommunityBrowser` which hike it is about and hands over the full route its own fetch produced (`previewOpened` / `previewLoaded` / `previewClosed`), and `routeLines` draws that one at full strength *instead of* its outline, so the map never carries two versions of one trail. It is drawn even when it is nowhere in the nearby answer, which is the case a hike found by typing its name is in — and `bringPreviewedRouteIntoView` fits the camera to it only when it is not already on screen, so a hiker who opened a hike by tapping its line keeps the context they chose it with and one who opened it from a search is taken to it. The three calls are matched on the listing because SwiftUI tears a replaced screen down *after* its replacement appears, so an unmatched close would blank the new preview's line on the way in. The browser reference the screen holds is written and never read, which is what keeps a screen presented over the map out of the map's redraw path. What replaces the sketch is `HikeDetailPreparation.prepare` — the same walk of the route, the same `StatGrid` and `StatTile`, so track points, elevation loss, moving speed and the start and end times read exactly as they do on a hike in the library, which is what somebody deciding whether to keep a stranger's trail is comparing against. The distance is `CommunityImport.routeLength`, not the listing's typed figure, for the reason the import uses it. Still no map of its own on that screen: tiles mean a provider, the entitlement check, the cache and a download, for a screen a hiker may back out of in two seconds.

**The share sheet's footer is held to what the upload actually carries.** `CommunityShareDisclosure` is a separate type from the view for that reason: the promise and the payload live in different files, and the first version of the screen said "nothing else from this hike" while `CommunityPublisher.share` copied the description and the date and the route carried a timestamp on every point. `CommunityShareDisclosureTests` asserts the wording against a real draft, so a field added to `CommunitySubmissionDraft` that nobody discloses fails a test rather than shipping.

**A suite must never reach the real transport.** There is no sandbox for a public database — a record written from a test run is a record every user can see, and it cannot be taken back. `OpenHikesModel.makeCommunityTransport()` returns `nil` under `AppLaunchEnvironment.isRunningTests`, which is the stricter guard than the `isHostingTests` the Live Activity controller uses, and UI automation is included for exactly this reason. A `nil` transport makes the *Community Hikes* section and the share button *absent* rather than disabled, and `makeCommunityBrowser(transport:blocks:)` withholds the geocoder from the same launches for the same reason.

**Sharing is collection, and the manifest says so.** `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` declares precise location, photos, and other user content, all linked to the user, because a submission carries a typed name and CloudKit stamps every record with its creator. `docs/privacy/` describes the same thing in the hiker's words. Both were previously able to say the app sends the developer nothing; neither may say that again while this feature exists.

**Reporting is an email, not a record type, and that follows from browsing being account-free.** The public database accepts a write only from an authenticated Apple Account — which is the same rule that makes `CommunityFailure.notSignedIn` a write-only failure — so no permission on any record type can let a signed-out hiker file a report, and a record-backed one would be missing for exactly the hikers the account-free browse flow exists for. `CommunityReport` therefore composes a `mailto:` on the device carrying the reason, the hiker's note, and **both** record names: deleting the `CommunityHike` unlists the hike and deleting the `CommunityHikeSubmission` removes the route and photographs behind it. The URL is built by hand rather than through `URLComponents.queryItems`, because `&` and `=` are legal in a query component and would silently truncate a note that contained one. It is in `CommunityHikeView`'s toolbar menu, alongside *Block*, and reachable in every phase, including a preview whose route never loaded — a title can be the objectionable part. It is deliberately *not* on `CommunityHikeRow`: a row carries a title, a distance and a name, and a report filed from one is about content the hiker has not seen. Nothing claims a report was *sent*, the same distinction the share sheet keeps between sent and published — and `openURL`'s `accepted` supports even less than it looks like it does: it says something opened the URL, not that a draft exists. Mail ships on every iPhone and is registered for the scheme, so a phone with **no account configured** accepts the URL, opens, and offers account setup; a discarded composer lands in the same place. So the handoff screen says *opened in* rather than *waiting in*, and neither outcome is a dead end — the message stays copyable and the form stays reachable from both, since the two cases this app cannot tell apart are exactly the ones where the hiker needs their text back. `CommunityReportTests` asserts what the reviewer receives, since that is the half that cannot be looked at.

**Blocking is device-local, keyed on the creator, and applied where the lists are read.** Guideline 1.2's other half (#249). It is not a report and does not take anything down: it hides one author's hikes for the hiker who blocked them. Three decisions hold it up. *Keyed on `CommunityHike.authorID`* — the creator CloudKit stamps on the submission, denormalised onto the listing at publication so the browse query has it, because `authorName` is free text the hiker types and a list keyed on it would block a string rather than a person and would fail open for anybody deliberately evading it; `CommunityListing.init(record:)` is therefore strict about `authorID` even though it renders nothing, since an unblockable listing is a rejection and a dropped one costs a row and a log line. *Device-local, in `UserDefaults` through `CommunityBlockList`* — browsing works signed out and a public-database write does not, the same rule that made reporting an email, so a CloudKit-backed block would be missing for exactly the hikers the account-free flow exists for; deliberately not in `SyncedSettings` either, so the list does not follow the hiker to a new phone. *Filtered twice, on purpose, and neither is redundant.* On **read**, `CommunityBrowser` keeps `nearbyResults`/`matchingResults` and exposes `nearbyListings`/`matchingListings` through one filter — that is what makes a block reach rows already on screen and an unblock give them back without a request, and what stops the two deliberately separate lists disagreeing about who is hidden. On **request**, both query methods take an `excluding: Set<String>` and the transport applies it before the `limit` is spent, because `limit` is a budget: twenty-five hikes by one blocked author would otherwise draw an empty list with an eligible twenty-sixth behind a cursor nobody follows, and asking the same question again would return the same hidden page forever. `CommunityPageBudget` bounds what that costs — one round trip when nobody is blocked, at most `maxRequests` when a page is eaten — and is a separate testable type for the reason `CommunityQueryPolicy` is: the behaviour is invisible in the result. `CommunityBrowser.refreshAfterBlock()` covers the remaining case, asking again only when a block took the last visible row. The affordance is a menu in `CommunityHikeView`'s toolbar next to *Report*, for the same reason reporting is on the screen showing the content and not on `CommunityHikeRow`; blocking pops the screen, since leaving it up would be the one place still showing what the hiker just hid. `BlockedHikersSection` in Settings names, dates and reverses each entry — a block a hiker can neither see nor undo is its own problem — and is absent rather than empty for anybody who has never blocked anyone.

**Publishing is behind the subscription; browsing, opening and saving are not.** Sharing a hike is the one paid thing the community feature does, and the split is deliberate: a published hike costs the public database's storage and every later reader's download for as long as it stands, which is the same recurring bill the commercial tile sources already put on the developer, while a list only paying customers could *read* would be a list not worth reading. The decision is `MapEntitlementState.publishTap`, which is the same three-way answer as a paid provider row and comes from the same private property so the two cannot drift — `.allow`, `.unlock` (the share button opens `MapPaywallView` instead of the form) and `.wait` (StoreKit has not answered, and the button is disabled and dimmed rather than swallowing the tap). It takes the **strict** reading of `.unknown`, more strictly than the map does: drawing a paid tile through the unresolved window costs a handful of tiles and is undone the moment StoreKit answers, while publishing writes a public record `CommunityTransporting` has no method to withdraw.

The gate is enforced in `CommunityPublisher.share` and not only at the button, because that is the one funnel every publish goes through and a gate living in a view is a gate the next caller does not know about; the entitlement is a parameter rather than a read of `MapEntitlement.current`, like every other `entitlement:` in this app, so a suite decides it outright. What that check is worth is worth stating plainly: **it is a client-side gate and holds for this app, not against a modified copy of it.** Nothing about payment changes what keeps an unreviewed route off other people's screens — that is the schema above, and only the schema.

Two consequences reach other files whenever this moves. `MapPaywallView` must list everything the subscription unlocks and unlock everything it lists, which is what App Review checks a subscription screen against, so a feature gated anywhere in the app adds a row there in the same change. And `MapEntitlementStore.productID` still reads `...pro.maps.monthly` though the subscription is no longer only about maps: the identifier is recorded against every past purchase and is the one string here that can never be corrected, which is exactly why the name a customer reads lives in the paywall's title instead.

**A hiker can see that their own hike went live, and cannot send it twice by accident.** Three states, derived in `CommunityPublicationState` from two columns on `Hike` rather than stored as a third that could disagree with them: `notShared`, `awaitingReview` (a `communitySubmissionID` with no `communityListingID`) and `published`. The share button draws one glyph each — `person.2`, `hourglass`, `person.2.fill` — and is **disabled** in the middle state, because a hike waiting for review has no action available at all: this app cannot withdraw a submission, amend one, or hurry anybody along, and leaving the button live would mean the only thing a tap could do is send a second copy.

`CommunityPublicationCheck.refresh` is the only thing that writes `communityListingID`. It asks `CommunityTransporting.publication(of:)` — one record, no cursor, no exclusion set — and only for a hike that has been sent and not yet seen live, so an unshared hike and an already-published one both cost nothing. It is silent on every failure, deliberately: it runs because a screen appeared rather than because anybody asked, so an offline phone goes on showing *waiting for review*, which is what it showed before and is still the most accurate thing anybody can say.

**`awaitingReview` covers a reviewer who declined, and the UI must never say otherwise.** A decline leaves no record, so the absence of a listing is the same absence either way. There are three states and not four; *rejected* would be an observation nothing supports. Publication is also **one-way** here — once a listing is seen it is remembered and never re-checked, so a takedown leaves the column stale, which is the cheap direction to be wrong in against a request per detail-open forever.

This costs **one more Console index**: `CommunityHike.submission` QUERYABLE. It is the only index here that browsing does not need, and it is safe for a reason worth keeping written down — querying it needs a submission's record name, which only its author has since nothing enumerates submissions, and what it returns is a listing that is `_world` read and already discoverable by location and title. The alternative, a status field on the submission for a reviewer to set, would put a writable field on the record type whose unwritability is the entire point of the schema.

Sharing an already-published hike stays possible, because it is the only way to publish an amended route, and the share form warns that it adds a second copy rather than replacing the first. A refusal would be wrong: the app cannot tell a stray second tap from a deliberate re-share, and cannot offer the replace-or-withdraw that would make the choice unnecessary.

**Still missing before this can ship.** Both halves of Guideline 1.2 are built — reporting (#248) and blocking (#249) — and the 24-hour commitment is described in `docs/privacy/`; the App Store listing has to describe them too. `CommunityHike.authorID` must exist in the Console **before the schema is deployed**, since a promoted field cannot be deleted, renamed or retyped, and the reviewer has to fill it in on every listing they publish or the hike will not appear. `CommunityHike.submission` must be QUERYABLE, or every shared hike reads as *waiting for review* forever however many are published. `CommunityHikeSubmission.routeOutline` needs no reviewer step at all — unlike `authorID`, the app writes it on upload and the map reads it back — but it **is in development already and is indexed**, which is the one thing it must not be, and stripping those three index keywords with an `import-schema` is a blocker on the press rather than a tidy-up after it. A submission uploaded before the field existed simply has no line; nothing has to be backfilled.

## Settled decisions — do not re-raise

Each of these looks like a finding and has already been investigated. Re-opening one needs new evidence, not a fresh reading of the same code.

**Types that should not become actors.** `TileCache`, whose `Mutex<MutationVersions>` makes bump-then-delete atomic against check-then-write whereas an actor's suspension points reintroduce the interleavings it exists to forbid. `HikePhotoStore`, whose only mutable state is an already-thread-safe `NSCache`, and where an actor would serialise thumbnail decodes that today run in parallel across gallery tiles. `SerialAsyncQueue`, because an actor gives mutual exclusion but explicitly not FIFO ordering across suspensions, and offers no barrier — both of which the "every fix accepted before now is on disk once the queue drains" invariant depends on. `SharedStore`, whose hazard is cross-process and therefore beyond in-process isolation; `options: .atomic` is the right answer and is used on every write. `RecordingStats` and `RecordingTrace`, read synchronously by `MapView.Coordinator` inside `withObservationTracking`, where isolation would put an `await` in the MapKit render path. And `PendingRecordingFixStore.withExclusiveLock`, whose `flock()` is cross-process and cannot be expressed by an actor.

**Older API that is justified, not legacy.** `MKMapView` behind `UIViewRepresentable` rather than SwiftUI `Map`: `Map` re-diffs its content builder on every `@Observable` change, which is the exact cost render isolation exists to avoid, and there is no SwiftUI equivalent for `MKUserTrackingButton` or for the `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `DirectionalPolylineRenderer` subclasses. `CLLocationManager` and its delegate rather than `CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates()`, which stalls after the first fix when the Simulator is driven by `simctl location … start`. The eight remaining GCD uses, each required by an API with no async form or by synchronous blocking work that should not be awaited — this is not a codebase that reached for GCD out of habit, since `Synchronization.Mutex` and `Atomic` appear across 14 files. `UIImagePickerController` for camera capture, whose camera source is not deprecated but is the system camera. The force unwraps of string-literal `URL(string:)` in `MapPurchaseLinks` and `TileAttribution`, wrapped in explicit lint pragmas. The `fatalError` in `OpenHikesModel` for a data store that cannot be created. And the 175 `canImport(UIKit)`/`#if os(iOS)` guards across 52 files, kept as the basis for a later platform target — unbuilt, not supported.

**A store-open failure is reported without attribution, on purpose.** Both the mirrored `Hike` store and the unmirrored `HikeLocalState` store are configurations of one `ModelContainer`, so a corrupt sidecar fails the open exactly as hard as a corrupt primary, and `StorageStartupIssue` carries only `underlyingDescription` — the two arrive as the same string. `loadContainer` catches, falls back to in-memory and raises the alert; the `fatalError` in `loadDefaultContainer` fires only if the in-memory fallback also fails, which is not a user-reachable path. Previous schemas have no supported upgrade path; see *Schema and migration policy*. Attributing an actual corrupt-store failure would need a second store-open on the launch path to produce a message the user cannot act on. `StorageStartupTests.failuresAreIndistinguishable` pins this so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

**The iCloud switch takes effect on the next launch, and that is the answer.** `cloudKitDatabase` is fixed when a `ModelConfiguration` is built, so `OpenHikesModel+Composition.swift` reads `SettingsKey.cloudSyncEnabled` once at launch and `CloudSyncCoordinator.pendingRelaunch` puts "Restart to Apply" in the settings row until the next one. Rebuilding the container in place was the alternative and it loses on the case that matters: `HikeRecorder` and `BackgroundTrailTracker` each hold the container they started with, `OpenHikesView` holds a `@State` `Hike` and every `@Query` below it holds more, and `HikeIntentCoordinator` was handed one into `AppDependencyManager` at launch — so a swap mid-session detaches all of them at once, and mid-*recording* it takes the store out from under a live trace and an open journal that only that store can finish. The prompt costs a hiker one relaunch; the swap costs them the walk. `CloudSyncRecordingTests` pins it at exactly that case — a recording crosses the flip untouched and lands whole, and the row is the only thing that changed — so this reads as a decision rather than an oversight. Settings are the half that does *not* wait: `SyncedSettingsMirror` rides on `NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore`, which the coordinator owns outright, and it starts and stops the moment the switch moves. Re-raising this needs a plan for the recording case, not a fresh reading of `ModelConfiguration`.

**Deliberate test seams, not production indirection.** The injectable transports, clocks, defaults, location sources, render boundaries and containers on `OverpassTrailGraphProvider`, `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `OfflineTileDownloader`, `CloudSyncCoordinator`, `LocationManager`, `MapEntitlementStore`, `TrailBasemapRenderer` and `TileSandbox` exist so suites never touch the app's singletons, the network or wall-clock time. That isolation did not go away with test parallelism: the whole bundle runs in one process, so a suite reaching for `TileCache.shared` would still leak into the next one. `TrailBasemapRenderer.Render` is the newest of them and the cautionary one: `MKMapSnapshotter` having no seam was true of the renderer rather than of the framework, and until it was fixed the basemap suite took four live snapshots per pass, asserted nothing about any of them, and cost 570 seconds of `maps.snapshot.timeout` against a 30-minute CI job — green the whole time. A live call fails no `#expect`, so `TrailBasemapRendererTests` carries a `.timeLimit` and a stub that records an issue when a render it forbids is attempted; those two, not an assertion on output, are what keep the boundary shut. The photo domain's ten small types are the same story — every one is under 250 lines with a single responsibility, and several exist because PhotoKit cannot be tested without a protocol seam. No collapse is recommended for either.

**Environment capabilities that are absent, not missing.** `StoreKitTest` cannot be used in this project, and the finding is the constraint rather than the suite. It needs a warnings-as-errors exemption merely to compile — Apple's own `SKTestTransaction.h` declares an `SKPaymentTransactionState` deprecated in iOS 18, and `SWIFT_TREAT_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS` reaches the Clang module build, so the `.pcm` fails to emit and nothing in the bundle compiles. `OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS = "$(inherited) -Xcc -Wno-error=deprecated-declarations"` on `OpenHikesTests` does fix that, and buys nothing: with the flag applied, `SKTestSession` still does not attach to `storekitd` under `xcodebuild test` on Xcode 26.6 / iOS 26.5. The session constructs, then `storefront` is empty rather than the `USA` in `OpenHikes.storekit`, `Product.products(for:)` returns nothing, `buyProduct` throws `notEntitled`, and storekitd logs the app talking to the *Sandbox* server — because the `.storekit` configuration is synced to the device by the Xcode IDE and not by the command line. App entitlements, stale daemon state and a `<StoreKitConfigurationFileReference>` in the scheme's TestAction were each ruled out by measurement. Separately, `AppStore.sync()` — which `restore()` is built on — never returns in a hosted unit test, observed past ten minutes, so a `restore()` test would hang the bundle rather than fail it. `MapEntitlementStoreLaunchTests`' header carries the whole argument; what *is* reachable is covered through the existing injectable seams.

**Claims investigated and found false.** The widget deep link does not need a `CFBundleURLTypes` registration; the system routes a `widgetURL` straight to the owning app, as `TrailWidgetDeepLink.swift` documents, so the scheme is only a label. A trim cannot delete a tile a concurrent auto-save just promoted: `trimCache` skips claimed names outright, and a tile promoted after the claim snapshot keeps its fetch-time mtime and so sorts last in the oldest-first deletion order. `RouteMotion` really is written by `RecordingPoint.routeCoordinate` and read by nothing but tests — the call sites that appear to read it read `RecordingMotionState` and `RecordingPointFlags.nonPedestrian`, which are different types. Syncing `tileProviderID` does not leave a keyless device with a blank map, because `TileProvider.renderable(id:)` falls back to the keyless default and `SettingsView.providerRow` compares against that effective provider. `Color+Hex` existing in both the app and the shared package is the ordinary cost of a widget target that cannot import the app, and `ColorHexTests` asserts parity between the two. And `PhotoLibraryReader` asking for `.readWrite` is correct rather than over-broad: `.addOnly` cannot read assets, and `.readWrite` is the only level that supports the limited-access flow. The bare `Task {}` calls on `@MainActor` types are not violations of the rule above: every one of them *is* main-actor work — a journal flush timer, a widget-fix merge into a `@MainActor` method, an `Observations` loop that calls `updateEnergyProfile()`, a hop into the `TrailBasemapRenderer` actor, a prefetch that then writes main-actor state — and the flagship example, `HikePhotoImport.discardFiles` reaching `erase()`, is already off-main because `HikePhotoStore.remove` calls `assertOffMainThread`. `Task.detached` would not even be the fix there: strip `@concurrent` from `erase()` and the callee becomes `@MainActor`, so the detached task hops straight back. The escape is `@concurrent` or `nonisolated` on the *callee*, which is what `scheduleLiveMatching` relies on. And `aps-environment = development` in `OpenHikes.entitlements` is correct in the tree: `CODE_SIGN_STYLE` is `Automatic`, so Xcode substitutes `production` on archive, and `development` is what a local build needs to register for push at all.

**Photo pixels stay on the device the photo was added on.** This is about the *private* database and the hiker's own hikes; the community feature publishes re-encoded copies to the *public* database, where the quota is the developer's, and that is not a re-opening of this — see *The community feature*. A `CKAsset`-backed column, a CloudKit record zone this app would own, and a fetch-on-demand path were each weighed against what they would spend, and the answer was no. Photo files are the largest thing this app writes; a walk carries dozens of them; and the private-database quota they would spend is the hiker's own iCloud storage, which is not this app's to enlarge. So `HikePhoto` stays what it is — where and when, a few dozen bytes — and the pixels stay files under `HikePhotoStore`, for the same reason `HikeLocalState` keeps the tile claim set device-local. "Added on" rather than "taken on" is the accurate half of that: `HikePhotoImport` copies a picked library asset into the local store exactly as the camera path does, so the device holding the only copy is the one the photo was *imported* on, which need not be the one that shot it. What follows is a state and not a bug: a second device holds photo rows whose files it will never have, permanently. That state is *said*, which is the part that was missing. `HikePhotoStore.hasImage(for:)` separates it from a file that is here and unreadable, `PhotoUnavailability` carries the two apart, and the strip's tile, the map callout and the viewer each name the one they are looking at — no placeholder that never resolves, no retry offered for a file nothing will send, and no "Remove Photo" pushed at a hiker on the device that is *not* the one with the picture, since that removal would take the row off every device. Re-opening this needs a measurement of what a walk's photos cost a real container, not a fresh reading of `@Attribute(.externalStorage)`.

**ActivityKit's own shape, worked around rather than fought.** `Activity<Attributes>` is a plain **non-Sendable class** whose `update` and `end` are `nonisolated async`, so holding one on a `@MainActor` type and awaiting a method on it is a region-isolation error — `SystemHikeActivityPresenter` boxes it in a `private nonisolated struct Handle: @unchecked Sendable` and crosses through two `nonisolated static` functions. The `nonisolated` on the box is load-bearing: `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor` would otherwise make the box itself main-actor isolated and the property unable to leave. `ActivityState` gained a `.pending` case in iOS 26, and with warnings as errors a non-exhaustive switch fails the build, so `isLive` names `.pending`, `.active` and `.stale` positively rather than defaulting. And the presenter *adopts* an already-running activity rather than requesting a second, because the system restores activities across a relaunch and a second request would leave two panels for one walk.

**A live recording outranks the selected trail, on every surface, without qualification.** The widget replaces the trail outright rather than showing the recording as a badge or a second line, and the reason is the same one `HikeLiveActivityController` gives for the Lock Screen: the two genuinely overlap — a hiker records their own track along an imported route — and only one of them would be *lost*, because a follow is re-derived from the trail and the next fix while a recording is not. A badge loses twice over: `systemSmall` has room for the live trace or for a trail, not both, and a secondary state is a second thing to keep fresh on a budget the recording feed is already spending. The rule is applied in exactly three places and they must keep agreeing — `TrailWidgetEntry.init`, `HikeLiveActivityController.accepts(_:)`, and `HikeRecordingControlState.init(snapshot:)`. It is total rather than conditional: a *paused* recording owns the widget too, because a lunch stop is still a walk and handing the screen back and then taking it away on the resume is the rule flickering rather than holding. Three questions get asked of one payload and only the first is ownership — *who owns the widget* (a recording exists), *whether it is worth spending on* (`isCapturingFixes`, which is what gates the twenty-minute timeline, the coarse location sample and the Smart Stack's `.fitness(.workoutActive)` relevance), and *what the Control Center button does* (a recording exists). A reader finding those three predicates different is looking at the policy, not at a bug. The takeover is a **projection and nothing else**: nothing on the widget side writes, so the stored trail and its basemaps survive untouched and the hiker's selection is back on the next timeline the moment `clearRecording` runs. That is what makes the budget half affordable — `TrailWidgetReload.requestUnlessRecording()` is the single gate the *trail* feed's redraws go through, because `BackgroundTrailTracker` publishes a live fix every 45 seconds against a recording snapshot `HikeRecorder.sharedSnapshotInterval` rewrites every fifteen minutes, so ungated the feed that has lost the screen spends the reload budget roughly twenty times faster than the one that holds it, on timelines that are byte-identical. The writes stay ungated on purpose; only the redraw waits. Two divergences are deliberate and are not the surfaces disagreeing. A *finished* recording lingers on the Lock Screen for `finishedDismissAfter` while the widget flips back to the trail at once — the panel is showing a result the hiker may not have seen yet, the widget is a glance at what is happening now. And the widget's takeover has **no staleness window**, unlike the panel's `recordingStaleAfter`: a recording payload left behind by a killed launch keeps the widget, keeps the twenty-minute timeline, and keeps sampling a coarse fix into `pending-fixes.json` — which is not a stale surface to be evicted but the recovery path working, since `mergeWidgetFixesAndReloadSession` is what folds those fixes back into the walk on the next launch. Adding an age bound would silently switch off gap filling for exactly the recordings that need it most. Re-raising any of this needs a design for the small family and a reload budget, not a fresh reading of `TrailWidgetEntry`.

**ActivityKit cannot be exercised from a hosted unit test.** Under `xcodebuild test`, `ActivityAuthorizationInfo` reports activities disabled and `Activity.request` throws; nothing makes either say otherwise, so a suite talking to the framework could only assert that nothing happened. Everything worth asserting is policy and sits above the `HikeActivityPresenting` seam, where `StubHikeActivityPresenter` watches it — which is also why `OpenHikesModel.makeLiveActivityController(defaults:)` returns `nil` under `AppLaunchEnvironment.isHostingTests` and the recorder and tracker both take the controller as an optional. UI tests, which run out of process, keep theirs.

**Assumptions that are load-bearing but unobserved.** MapKit is assumed to re-enter `draw` after every `setNeedsDisplay(_ mapRect:)` and to be the only thing that invalidates a tile; the whole overzoom path rests on both, and the redraw loop `CachingTileOverlayRenderer.fetchPath(drawing:maximumZ:isCached:)` closes was reasoned about rather than observed under Instruments, as was the blank sibling that closing it exposed. `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` on `Hike.route` and `Hike.rawRoute` is assumed to be what makes mirroring carry them as a `CKAsset` rather than a record field — documented behaviour that compiles, but nothing here has watched a twenty-thousand-point route cross a real container.

**Two foreground location managers, deliberately.** `LocationManager` and `SystemRecordingLocationSource` each own a `CLLocationManager`, and both receive updates during a recording. Verified rather than assumed: the foreground manager never stops once started, and the recording source asks for `kCLLocationAccuracyBest` with a 10 m filter against the foreground manager's baseline. iOS coalesces same-process location demand to the most demanding request, so this does not imply twice the GPS hardware power; what it duplicates is delegate dispatch and authorization handling, and both deliver through `onMainActor` so it costs no `Task` per fix. The separation is what keeps background semantics — `allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates`, a `CLBackgroundActivitySession`, no automatic pausing — from leaking into ordinary map browsing. Revisit only if a device energy trace shows meaningful CPU overhead, and preserve those background semantics if the two are ever consolidated.

## Documentation

Three files with distinct jobs, plus the issue tracker. Keep a fact in exactly
one of them.

- `README.md` is for someone who just found the repository: what the app is, what it needs, how to build and run it, and how it is laid out. Engineering rationale does not belong there.
- `AGENTS.md` is a pointer, not a source: it sends an agent here and repeats only the handful of rules that are tripped over before this file is read. Anything it says has to already be true here.
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` — this file — holds the durable conventions, commands, architecture rules and settled decisions, including all migration/reset policy and CloudKit schema deployment notes.
- `PERFORMANCE.md` is a **live list, not a log**. A finding that has been fixed is deleted rather than annotated, and a claim that stopped matching the code is deleted whether or not anything was done about it. It is not a changelog; git already is one.
- `docs/` is the published GitHub Pages site (`main:/docs`) and nothing else: `privacy/` and `terms/`, the two pages the App Store listing links. It is not a documentation folder. `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md` lived there and were served as raw markdown — `.nojekyll` means nothing in `docs/` is rendered — while their actual readers were on github.com; both are at the repository root now, beside `README.md` and `SECURITY.md`. A new prose document belongs at the root; only something the website serves belongs in `docs/`.
- **Open work lives in GitHub issues, not in a checked-in list.** Missing features, product decisions that are still open, and claims no test can settle are issues on `ZsomborRajki/OpenHikes`. A document does not accumulate a to-do list beside them.

Cite these documents from source comments by *section name*, never by finding number or quoted figure. Numbered citations went stale within a single revision — comments referring to "Finding 1" and "Finding 2" survived the findings being renumbered, and quoted millisecond figures the documents no longer contained.
